Overall, this paper presents a valuable contribution to the field of image segmentation by addressing the challenge of realistic image normalization in multi-domain scenarios.

This paper presents a method for realistic image normalization in the context of multi-domain segmentation. Image normalization is an important preprocessing step in many computer vision tasks, including segmentation. However, existing methods often fail to account for variations in lighting, color, and texture across different domains. The proposed method addresses this issue by learning a domain-specific normalization function using a generative adversarial network. The effectiveness of the proposed method is demonstrated through extensive experiments on two real-world datasets, showing significant improvements in segmentation performance compared to existing normalization methods. The paper concludes by discussing the implications of the proposed method and potential directions for future research in this area.

Semantic image segmentation is a fundamental task in computer vision that aims to assign a semantic label to each pixel in an image. Deep learning methods have achieved remarkable success in this field, but real-time performance remains a challenge. This paper presents a comprehensive survey of deep learning methods for semantic image segmentation in real-time. We review various architectures, such as fully convolutional networks (FCNs), encoder-decoder networks, and dilated convolutions, and discuss their advantages and limitations. We also analyze different strategies for improving real-time performance, including network compression, parallel processing, and hardware acceleration. Furthermore, we provide an overview of benchmark datasets and evaluation metrics commonly used in this domain. Finally, we discuss open challenges and future directions for real-time semantic image segmentation using deep learning methods. This survey serves as a valuable resource for researchers and practitioners working in the field of computer vision and deep learning.

Semantic image segmentation is the task of assigning meaningful labels to each pixel in an image. Deep learning models have shown promising results in achieving accurate and reliable semantic image segmentation. This survey paper provides a comprehensive overview of various state-of-the-art deep learning methods for semantic image segmentation in real-time. The paper discusses different network architectures, loss functions, data augmentation techniques, and evaluation metrics used in the field. Furthermore, the paper highlights challenges and limitations in existing methods and proposes future research directions. Overall, this survey provides valuable insights for researchers and practitioners working in the field of semantic image segmentation.

In recent years, deep learning has shown promising results in various medical image segmentation tasks. However, most existing methods focus on 2D image segmentation and do not fully exploit the spatial information in 3D medical images. In this paper, we propose a novel architecture called UXNet for 3D medical image segmentation. UXNet utilizes a multi-level feature aggregation strategy to capture both local and global contextual information. Specifically, it consists of a feature extraction module, a multi-level feature aggregation module, and a segmentation module. The feature extraction module extracts high-level features from the input 3D medical image. The multi-level feature aggregation module aggregates features from different levels of the feature extraction module to capture both local and global contextual information. Finally, the segmentation module generates the segmentation mask based on the aggregated features. Experimental results on a publicly available dataset demonstrate that UXNet achieves state-of-the-art performance in 3D medical image segmentation tasks. The proposed architecture shows great potential for improving the accuracy and efficiency of medical image segmentation, which can benefit various clinical applications.

In the field of medical image segmentation, the accurate segmentation of 3D medical images plays a crucial role in clinical decision-making. However, achieving accurate segmentation remains challenging due to the complexity and variability of medical images. In this paper, we propose a novel method called UXNet for 3D medical image segmentation. UXNet aims to improve the performance of segmentation by searching for multi-level feature aggregation. To achieve this, UXNet combines the strengths of both deep neural networks and convolutional neural networks, leveraging their ability to extract rich and meaningful features from medical images. We evaluate UXNet on several benchmark datasets and compare its performance against state-of-the-art methods. The experimental results demonstrate that UXNet outperforms existing methods in terms of segmentation accuracy and efficiency. Therefore, we conclude that UXNet is a promising approach for 3D medical image segmentation and has the potential to contribute to the field of clinical decision-making.

This paper proposes a novel approach for domain generalization in style transfer tasks by integrating shape and spatial information. The authors introduce a Random Style Transfer based Domain Generalization Network (RST-DGN) that leverages a random style transfer module to generate diverse style images. These style images are then used to train a domain generalization network that learns to extract shape and spatial information from the input images. Experimental results on various datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach in improving the generalization performance of style transfer models across different domains. The RST-DGN achieves state-of-the-art performance and outperforms existing methods in terms of both visual quality and domain generalization capability. Overall, this paper presents a promising solution for addressing the domain shift problem in style transfer tasks.

In this paper, the authors propose a novel approach to domain generalization (DG) in computer vision using random style transfer. The goal of DG is to improve the performance of models trained on a source domain when applied to a target domain with variations in shape and spatial information. The proposed method combines shape and spatial information by randomly transferring styles between source and target domains. The authors evaluate their method on several benchmark datasets and compare it with existing DG techniques. The results show that their approach achieves superior performance in terms of accuracy and robustness against variations in shape and spatial information. This work contributes to the field of computer vision by providing a new perspective on DG and demonstrating the potential of random style transfer for improving model generalization in diverse domains.

This paper presents a framework called MCU-Net that aims to improve decision support systems for patient referrals in healthcare contexts by incorporating uncertainty representations. The framework utilizes a combination of deep learning models and probabilistic graphical models to capture and represent uncertainties in the decision-making process. The authors demonstrate the effectiveness of MCU-Net through experiments on a real-world dataset, showing that it outperforms existing methods in terms of accuracy and reliability. The results suggest that incorporating uncertainty representations can enhance the decision-making process in healthcare and improve patient outcomes.

This paper proposes a framework called MCU-Net for representing and handling uncertainties in decision support systems for patient referrals in healthcare contexts. The framework introduces a novel way to model and quantify uncertainty using a combination of Multiple Convolutional Uncertainty Networks (MCUNet) and Bayesian neural networks (BNN). The authors demonstrate the effectiveness of the framework by evaluating it on a real-world dataset of patient referrals in a healthcare setting. Results show that the MCU-Net framework achieves superior performance in uncertain scenarios compared to existing approaches. This research contributes to the field by providing a reliable and interpretable approach for modeling uncertainties in healthcare decision support systems, which can assist healthcare professionals in making informed referral decisions.

Semantic video segmentation is a challenging task that requires accurate and efficient processing of large amounts of video data. In this paper, we propose TapLab, a fast framework for semantic video segmentation that leverages compressed-domain knowledge. TapLab utilizes a tap-based approach to efficiently process video frames by tapping into compressed-domain information. We introduce a TapNet architecture that combines a tap-based encoder-decoder network with a compressed-domain feature extractor. Our experiments demonstrate that TapLab achieves state-of-the-art performance in terms of both accuracy and speed on various benchmark datasets. Furthermore, we show that TapLab is robust to compression artifacts and can effectively handle videos with different compression levels. Overall, TapLab provides a fast and efficient solution for semantic video segmentation by exploiting compressed-domain knowledge.

This paper presents TapLab, a fast framework for semantic video segmentation that leverages compressed-domain knowledge. In contrast to existing approaches that operate on uncompressed videos, TapLab directly processes compressed videos to achieve real-time performance. The proposed framework utilizes compressed-domain knowledge such as motion vectors and macroblock types to assist the segmentation process. Experimental results demonstrate that TapLab achieves competitive segmentation accuracy compared to state-of-the-art methods, while significantly reducing computation time. Additionally, the framework is highly scalable and can be easily adapted for different video codecs and resolutions. This work showcases the potential of tapping into compressed-domain knowledge for efficient semantic video segmentation.

This paper proposes a domain adaptive medical image segmentation method using adversarial learning of disease-specific spatial patterns. The method aims to address the challenge of limited labeled data in medical image segmentation tasks by leveraging unlabeled data from different domains. The proposed approach consists of two main components: a segmentation network and a domain adaptation network. The segmentation network is trained to perform pixel-wise segmentation on labeled data, while the domain adaptation network learns to align the feature distributions between the labeled and unlabeled data. The domain adaptation network includes a generator and a discriminator, which are trained in an adversarial manner to generate domain-invariant features. Experimental results on two medical image segmentation datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in improving segmentation performance on unseen domains. The proposed approach shows promise in addressing the domain shift problem in medical image segmentation and has the potential to improve the generalization capability of segmentation models in clinical practice.

This academic paper proposes a domain adaptive medical image segmentation technique through the use of adversarial learning for disease-specific spatial patterns. The proposed method incorporates a segmentation network and a discriminator network that are jointly trained to achieve accurate and robust segmentation across different medical domains. The discriminator network is trained to distinguish between real and generated image segments, while the segmentation network is trained to generate image segments that can fool the discriminator. This adversarial training approach enables the segmentation network to learn disease-specific spatial patterns that are transferable across different domains, resulting in improved segmentation performance. Experimental results on two large-scale medical image datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and generalizability of the proposed method compared to existing approaches. Overall, this paper addresses the challenge of domain adaptation in medical image segmentation and presents a novel solution based on adversarial learning.

Medical image segmentation is a critical task in various clinical applications, but it is often challenging due to the inherent uncertainty in the segmentation process. In this paper, we propose a novel approach for uncertainty quantification in medical image segmentation using normalizing flows. Normalizing flows are a flexible class of generative models that can capture complex distributions. We adapt normalizing flows to the task of medical image segmentation by training them to model the posterior distribution of the segmentation given the input image. We then use the trained normalizing flows to estimate the uncertainty in the segmentation by sampling from the posterior distribution. We evaluate our approach on a dataset of brain MRI scans and compare it to existing uncertainty quantification methods. Our results demonstrate that our method provides accurate and reliable uncertainty estimates, which can be valuable for clinical decision-making and downstream analysis. Overall, our work contributes to the field of medical image segmentation by providing a principled and effective approach for uncertainty quantification.

Medical image segmentation is an important task in clinical practice, as it enables the accurate delineation of anatomical structures, which is crucial for diagnosis and treatment planning. However, uncertainties associated with the segmentation process can lead to potential errors and inconsistencies. In this paper, we propose a method for uncertainty quantification in medical image segmentation using normalizing flows. Normalizing flows are flexible generative models that can learn complex distributions. We apply normalizing flows to the task of medical image segmentation by mapping the input image to a joint space of segmentation, uncertainty, and latent variables. Through experiments on various medical imaging datasets, we demonstrate that our method effectively captures uncertainties and provides reliable segmentation maps. Our approach has the potential to improve medical image segmentation by providing clinicians with uncertainty information, enabling them to make more informed decisions.

This paper presents an end-to-end trainable deep active contour model for automated image segmentation, specifically focusing on delineating buildings in aerial imagery. The proposed model combines the strengths of deep learning and active contour models to achieve accurate and efficient segmentation results. The model is trained using a large dataset of aerial imagery and ground truth annotations. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed model outperforms existing methods in terms of segmentation accuracy and computational efficiency. The paper also discusses the potential applications of the proposed model in various domains, such as urban planning and disaster response. Overall, this work contributes to the field of automated image segmentation by introducing a novel approach that can effectively delineate buildings in aerial imagery.

Accurately segmenting buildings in aerial imagery is a challenging task due to variations in building shapes, sizes, and textures. In this paper, we propose an end-to-end trainable deep active contour model for automated image segmentation. We leverage recent advancements in deep learning to enhance the traditional active contour model by incorporating convolutional and recurrent neural networks. Our model is trained on a large dataset of aerial imagery and is capable of accurately delineating buildings in unseen images. We evaluate the performance of our model against existing methods on a benchmark dataset, and demonstrate superior accuracy and efficiency. Our proposed approach has the potential to aid in various applications such as urban planning and disaster response.

This paper presents AinnoSeg, a novel approach for panoramic segmentation with high performance. The proposed method utilizes a deep learning framework to achieve accurate and efficient segmentation of panoramic images. AinnoSeg incorporates a panoramic feature extraction module to capture the unique characteristics of panoramic images, followed by a segmentation module that utilizes a modified U-Net architecture. The proposed method achieves state-of-the-art performance on various benchmark datasets, outperforming existing methods in terms of both accuracy and computational efficiency. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of AinnoSeg in various segmentation tasks, including object segmentation and semantic segmentation. The proposed method has the potential to be applied in various real-world applications, such as autonomous driving and virtual reality.

AinnoSeg is a deep learning-based approach for panoramic segmentation that achieves high performance on both speed and accuracy. Panoramic images require specialized segmentation methods due to their unique 360-degree field of view. AinnoSeg uses a fully convolutional network with a U-Net architecture to capture spatial and contextual information in panoramic images. It incorporates an attention mechanism to prioritize important regions for better segmentation results. Additionally, AinnoSeg introduces a new loss function that combines focal loss and IoU loss to improve accuracy. Experimental results on benchmark datasets demonstrate that AinnoSeg outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of segmentation accuracy, while also achieving faster processing times. This makes it a valuable tool for applications such as panoramic image editing and virtual reality content creation.

Semantic image segmentation is a challenging task in computer vision that involves assigning a label to each pixel in an image. While single stage encoder-decoder networks have achieved impressive results in this domain, they often struggle with capturing fine-grained details and producing accurate boundaries. In this paper, we propose a novel approach called deep decoders for semantic image segmentation. Our method involves incorporating multiple decoder modules into the network architecture, each responsible for capturing different levels of detail. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on several benchmark datasets, achieving state-of-the-art performance in terms of both accuracy and boundary quality. Furthermore, we conduct extensive ablation studies to analyze the impact of different decoder configurations and provide insights into the strengths and weaknesses of our method. Overall, our work highlights the importance of incorporating deep decoders into the network design for improved semantic image segmentation.

Semantic image segmentation is a crucial task in computer vision, as it aims to classify each pixel in an image into a specific class. This paper proposes a novel approach for semantic image segmentation using deep decoders. Unlike traditional single stage encoder-decoder networks, the proposed model utilizes a multi-stage architecture that includes multiple parallel decoders. Each decoder learns to extract different levels of semantic information from the intermediate feature maps generated by the encoder. The final segmentation map is obtained by fusing the outputs of all decoders using a fusion module. Experimental results on various benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach, achieving state-of-the-art performance in terms of segmentation accuracy and boundary detection. The proposed deep decoders offer a promising direction for improving semantic image segmentation and can be easily integrated into existing network architectures.

Semantic segmentation is a crucial task in computer vision, but it often suffers from limited data and annotations, which hinders the performance of existing models. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to tackle this problem by leveraging unsupervised learning and transfer learning techniques. We first use unsupervised learning to generate pseudo-labels for the unlabeled data, which helps to increase the size of the training set. Then, we employ transfer learning to transfer knowledge from a pre-trained model to the target task of semantic segmentation. Our experimental results on benchmark datasets demonstrate that our approach significantly improves the performance of semantic segmentation models, even with limited data and annotations. This work provides a promising solution to address the challenges of limited data and annotations in semantic segmentation, and opens up new possibilities for future research in this area.

This paper addresses the challenge of limited data and annotations in semantic segmentation. Semantic segmentation is a task in computer vision that involves assigning semantic labels to each pixel in an image. The performance of semantic segmentation models heavily depends on the availability and quality of data and annotations for training. However, creating large-scale, high-quality annotated datasets for semantic segmentation is time-consuming and expensive. 

The authors propose several strategies to tackle the problem of limited data and annotations in semantic segmentation. First, they propose a semi-supervised learning framework that combines limited labeled data with a large amount of unlabeled data. The model is trained on both labeled and unlabeled data to leverage the additional information in the unlabeled samples. 

Next, the authors introduce a novel data augmentation technique specifically designed for semantic segmentation. This technique generates synthetic training samples by transforming the available labeled data while preserving the semantic labels. The augmented dataset is then used to train the model, improving its performance and generalization capabilities.

Additionally, the authors propose a weakly supervised approach to semantic segmentation that reduces the reliance on fully annotated data. Instead of pixel-level annotations, they use image-level labels or bounding box annotations to train the model. This approach allows for faster and cheaper annotation processes while still achieving competitive segmentation results.

The effectiveness of the proposed strategies is validated through extensive experiments on benchmark datasets. The experimental results demonstrate that the proposed techniques improve the performance of semantic segmentation models even when limited data and annotations are available. The findings contribute to the field of computer vision by providing practical solutions to address the challenges posed by limited data and annotations in semantic segmentation.

This paper proposes a novel approach for instrument segmentation in robotic surgery using unsupervised learning with cycle-consistent adversarial networks (CycleGANs). The goal is to automatically segment surgical instruments from the background in surgical videos without the need for manual annotations. The proposed method leverages the cycle-consistency property of CycleGANs to learn a mapping between the instrument and background domains, enabling the generation of synthetic instrument images from background images and vice versa. The generated synthetic images are then used to train a segmentation model, which is evaluated on a dataset of real surgical videos. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach in accurately segmenting instruments in robotic surgery, highlighting its potential for improving surgical workflow and assisting surgeons in real-time.

This paper presents a novel approach towards unsupervised learning for instrument segmentation in robotic surgery using cycle-consistent adversarial networks (CycleGANs). Instrument segmentation is a crucial task in robotic surgery to enable surgical robots to autonomously identify and track surgical instruments during surgery. However, obtaining labeled training data for instrument segmentation is challenging and time-consuming. In this work, we propose an unsupervised learning framework that leverages CycleGANs to learn a mapping between real surgical images and synthetic images with instrument annotations. By training on this synthetic data, the model can then be applied to real surgical images for instrument segmentation. The proposed method is evaluated on a dataset of laparoscopic videos and achieves promising results, demonstrating the potential of unsupervised learning for instrument segmentation in robotic surgery. The proposed framework has the potential to greatly improve the efficiency and accuracy of instrument segmentation in robotic surgery, leading to improved surgical outcomes and patient safety.

This paper presents a novel approach for medical image segmentation using a technique called Meta Corrupted Pixels Mining (MCPM). The proposed method leverages the concept of corrupted pixels to improve the accuracy and efficiency of segmentation algorithms. The MCPM algorithm first identifies corrupted pixels in the input image and then uses these pixels to guide the segmentation process. Experimental results on a dataset of medical images demonstrate that the MCPM algorithm outperforms state-of-the-art segmentation methods in terms of both accuracy and computational efficiency. The proposed approach has the potential to significantly improve the performance of medical image segmentation algorithms, leading to more accurate and reliable diagnoses in the field of medical imaging.

Medical image segmentation plays a crucial role in medical diagnosis and treatment planning. However, existing segmentation algorithms often suffer from limited accuracy and computational efficiency. In this paper, we propose a novel approach called Meta Corrupted Pixels Mining (MCPM) for medical image segmentation. MCPM leverages the idea of meta learning and corrupted pixels mining to improve segmentation accuracy. Specifically, MCPM first generates a set of corrupted pixels by randomly perturbing the original image, which serves as a meta task to train a meta model. The corrupted pixels are then used to guide the segmentation process through a two-stage training scheme. Experimental results on several medical image datasets demonstrate that MCPM achieves significant improvements in both segmentation accuracy and computational efficiency compared to state-of-the-art methods. The proposed approach has the potential to improve the quality of medical image segmentation and facilitate more accurate diagnosis and treatment planning in clinical practice.

This paper proposes a novel image segmentation method based on Kullback-Leibler divergence-based fuzzy C-means clustering, incorporating morphological reconstruction and wavelet frames. The proposed method aims to overcome the limitations of traditional image segmentation techniques by integrating the advantages of fuzzy clustering, morphological reconstruction, and wavelet frames. The Kullback-Leibler divergence is used as a similarity measure to improve the accuracy of the clustering process. Morphological reconstruction is employed to enhance the segmentation results by removing noise and preserving object boundaries. Wavelet frames are utilized to capture both local and global image features, enabling more accurate segmentation. Experimental results on various benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and superiority of the proposed method compared to state-of-the-art image segmentation techniques.

Image segmentation plays a crucial role in many computer vision and image processing applications. This paper presents a novel approach to image segmentation using a combination of fuzzy $C$-means clustering, morphological reconstruction, and wavelet frames. The proposed method uses Kullback-Leibler divergence as a similarity measure for clustering, which allows for more accurate segmentation results. Additionally, morphological reconstruction is used to enhance the quality of the segmentation by removing noise and fine structures. The use of wavelet frames further improves the segmentation by capturing both high-frequency and low-frequency information in the image. Experimental results on various benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and superiority of the proposed method compared to other state-of-the-art approaches.

This paper presents a novel approach for anatomically plausible segmentation using post-processing with denoising autoencoders (DAEs). The proposed method aims to improve the accuracy and robustness of segmentation algorithms by incorporating DAEs into the post-processing stage. The DAEs are trained to denoise the segmentation masks generated by the initial segmentation algorithm, thereby reducing the impact of noise and artifacts. Experimental results on various medical imaging datasets demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves superior segmentation performance compared to state-of-the-art methods. The findings suggest that post-processing with DAEs can effectively enhance the quality of segmentation results and improve the reliability of medical image analysis.

Automated segmentation of anatomical structures from medical images is of great importance in various clinical applications. However, the accuracy and efficiency of existing segmentation methods can be limited due to the presence of noise and artifacts in the image data. In this paper, we propose a novel approach called Post-DAE that utilizes denoising autoencoders to improve the segmentation results. The idea is to first pre-train a denoising autoencoder on a large dataset of noisy and clean image pairs, and then use the learned features to post-process the segmentation outputs from a traditional segmentation algorithm. Experimental results on a dataset of brain MRI images demonstrate that the proposed Post-DAE method achieves significantly better segmentation accuracy compared to several state-of-the-art segmentation methods. Furthermore, the computational efficiency of the method is also improved due to the reduced need for manual intervention and parameter tuning. Overall, the results suggest that the proposed method holds great potential for improving the accuracy and efficiency of anatomical segmentation in medical imaging.

Cardiac segmentation is a crucial step in medical image analysis for diagnosing and treating cardiovascular diseases. However, accurate and robust segmentation remains challenging due to the complex anatomical structures and variations in cardiac images. In this paper, we propose a novel approach for cardiac segmentation that incorporates strong anatomical guarantees. Our method leverages a deep learning framework combined with a graph-based optimization algorithm to achieve accurate and consistent segmentation results. We evaluate our approach on a large dataset of cardiac images and compare it with state-of-the-art methods. The experimental results demonstrate that our method outperforms existing approaches in terms of segmentation accuracy and robustness. Furthermore, our approach provides strong anatomical guarantees, ensuring that the segmented regions adhere to the expected cardiac anatomy. Overall, our proposed method has the potential to improve the accuracy and reliability of cardiac segmentation in clinical practice.

This paper presents a deep learning based approach for cardiac segmentation with strong anatomical guarantees. The proposed method consists of a fully convolutional neural network that is trained using annotated cardiac MRI images. Additionally, the network incorporates a conditional random field model to incorporate anatomical constraints into the segmentation process. The experimental results demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on a publicly available cardiac MRI dataset. The strong anatomical guarantees provided by the model ensure accurate and reliable segmentation of various cardiac structures, which is crucial for clinical diagnosis and treatment planning. The proposed method has the potential to improve the efficiency and accuracy of cardiac segmentation in clinical practice.

This paper presents a Bayesian optimization approach for modular black-box systems with switching costs. The authors propose a novel algorithm that combines Bayesian optimization with a switching cost model to efficiently search for the optimal configuration of a modular system. The algorithm uses a Gaussian process regression model to model the performance of each module and a Bayesian optimization framework to guide the search process. The switching cost model is used to account for the costs associated with switching between different module configurations. The authors evaluate the proposed algorithm on a set of benchmark problems and demonstrate its effectiveness in finding near-optimal solutions with reduced switching costs. The results show that the algorithm outperforms existing approaches in terms of solution quality and computational efficiency. Overall, this paper provides a valuable contribution to the field of modular system optimization and offers a practical solution for optimizing modular black-box systems with switching costs.

In this paper, we propose a novel approach for optimizing modular black-box systems with switching costs using Bayesian optimization. Modular black-box systems consist of multiple independent subsystems, each with its own design parameters and performance metrics. Switching costs arise when a decision is made to switch from one subsystem to another. Our approach aims to simultaneously optimize the design parameters of each subsystem while considering the switching costs. We develop a Bayesian optimization algorithm that incorporates a switching cost model, allowing us to effectively explore the design space and minimize the overall cost. We evaluate the performance of our approach on a set of synthetic and real-world modular black-box systems and demonstrate its effectiveness in finding optimal solutions with minimal switching costs. Our results indicate that our approach outperforms existing optimization methods in this domain and has the potential to be applied to a wide range of modular black-box systems.

Image segmentation is a fundamental task in computer vision that involves partitioning an image into meaningful regions. Over the years, deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have emerged as a powerful tool for image segmentation due to their ability to learn hierarchical representations. This paper presents a comprehensive survey of the evolution of image segmentation using deep CNNs. We review the key milestones in the development of CNN-based segmentation methods, including early approaches such as fully convolutional networks (FCNs) and U-Net, as well as more recent advancements such as dilated convolutions and attention mechanisms. We also discuss the challenges and limitations of CNN-based segmentation methods, such as the need for large annotated datasets and the difficulty in handling class imbalance. Finally, we highlight potential future directions for research in this field, including the integration of domain knowledge and the exploration of novel network architectures. Overall, this survey provides a valuable resource for researchers and practitioners interested in understanding the state-of-the-art in image segmentation using deep CNNs.

This paper surveys the evolution of image segmentation techniques using deep convolutional neural networks. Image segmentation is a fundamental task in computer vision and has numerous applications across various domains. Deep convolutional neural networks have demonstrated remarkable performance in image segmentation tasks, replacing traditional methods that relied on handcrafted features and heuristics. This paper aims to provide a comprehensive survey of the field, discussing the evolution of image segmentation techniques from classical methods to the recent advancements using deep convolutional neural networks. The survey covers various aspects such as different network architectures, loss functions, training strategies, and evaluation metrics. Additionally, the paper discusses the challenges and limitations faced by the current state-of-the-art approaches and identifies potential directions for future research in this field. Overall, this survey serves as a valuable resource for researchers and practitioners interested in understanding the evolution of image segmentation techniques using deep convolutional neural networks.

This paper presents a novel approach for learning to segment objects from misaligned and partial labels. Traditional methods for image segmentation rely on accurate and complete annotations, which can be time-consuming and expensive to obtain. In this work, we propose a framework that leverages weakly labeled data, where only a subset of pixels are annotated and the annotations may be misaligned with the true object boundaries. Our approach combines a convolutional neural network with a graph-based optimization algorithm to iteratively refine the segmentation mask. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on several benchmark datasets and show that it outperforms existing approaches in terms of segmentation accuracy. Our framework has the potential to significantly reduce the annotation effort required for training segmentation models, making it more accessible and practical for real-world applications.

The paper proposes a novel method for learning to segment images when the training data consists of misaligned and partial labels. Traditional segmentation methods rely on accurate and complete annotation, which is often challenging and time-consuming to obtain. In this paper, we introduce a new approach that leverages weakly supervised learning techniques to address the issue of misaligned and incomplete annotations. Specifically, we propose a dual task network that simultaneously learns to predict both the class labels and the alignment offsets. By jointly training these two tasks, our model is able to effectively overcome the challenges associated with misalignment and partial labeling. Experimental results on a number of benchmark datasets demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms existing approaches in terms of segmentation accuracy and robustness to label noise. Overall, our work contributes to the field of image segmentation by improving the reliability and efficiency of annotation in the presence of misaligned and partial labels.

This paper presents a novel approach called ECG-DelNet for the delineation of ambulatory electrocardiograms (ECGs) with mixed quality labeling using neural networks. The proposed method utilizes a deep learning architecture that combines convolutional and recurrent neural networks to accurately detect and delineate the QRS complex, P wave, and T wave in ECG signals. The network is trained on a dataset of ambulatory ECGs with mixed quality labeling, which includes both manually annotated and automatically labeled data. Experimental results demonstrate that ECG-DelNet achieves superior performance compared to existing methods, with high accuracy and low computational cost. The proposed approach has the potential to improve the accuracy and efficiency of ECG delineation in clinical practice, enabling more accurate diagnosis and monitoring of cardiovascular diseases.

This paper presents a novel approach for accurately delineating ambulatory electrocardiograms (ECG) by using neural networks. The proposed method, called ECG-DelNet, is designed to handle the challenges posed by mixed quality labeling in ambulatory ECG data. ECG-DelNet consists of a multi-scale convolutional neural network (CNN) architecture that leverages both global and local contextual information for accurate delineation of ECG signals. The model is trained on a dataset comprising ambulatory ECG data with mixed quality labeling, which simulates real-world scenarios. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of ECG-DelNet in accurately delineating ECG signals, even in the presence of mixed quality labeling. The proposed method can potentially improve the accuracy and efficiency of ambulatory ECG analysis in clinical settings.

This paper introduces a novel approach to multitask learning called partly supervised multitask learning. Traditional multitask learning methods assume that all tasks have labeled data available for training, which is often not the case in real-world scenarios. In partly supervised multitask learning, some tasks have labeled data while others do not. The proposed method leverages the labeled data from the available tasks to learn a shared representation that can be used to improve the performance on the tasks with missing labels. Experimental results on various datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach compared to traditional multitask learning methods. The findings suggest that partly supervised multitask learning can be a valuable tool in scenarios where labeled data is limited or unavailable for some tasks.

This paper introduces partly supervised multitask learning, a novel approach for leveraging both labeled and unlabeled data in a multitask learning scenario. Traditional multitask learning methods rely heavily on labeled data for all tasks in order to achieve good generalization performance. However, acquiring labeled data can be expensive and time-consuming, making it impractical for many real-world applications. In this paper, we propose a framework that combines labeled data with a small amount of labeled data to improve the performance of multitask learning. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method through experiments on several benchmark datasets, showing significant improvements in performance compared to traditional multitask learning approaches. Our results suggest that partly supervised multitask learning can be a valuable tool for leveraging unlabeled data in multitask learning scenarios.

Cell image segmentation is a crucial task in biomedical image analysis, as it enables the quantification and analysis of cellular structures. In this paper, we propose a novel deep learning architecture called Feedback U-net for cell image segmentation. The proposed architecture incorporates a feedback mechanism that allows the model to iteratively refine its predictions. This feedback mechanism is achieved by introducing skip connections between the encoder and decoder blocks of the U-net architecture. Additionally, we introduce a novel loss function that combines both pixel-wise and boundary-aware terms to improve the accuracy of the segmentation. We evaluate the performance of the Feedback U-net on several benchmark datasets and compare it with other state-of-the-art methods. The experimental results demonstrate that the proposed architecture achieves superior performance in terms of segmentation accuracy and boundary delineation. Furthermore, we conduct ablation studies to analyze the impact of different components of the Feedback U-net architecture. Overall, our findings suggest that the Feedback U-net is a promising approach for cell image segmentation and has the potential to advance the field of biomedical image analysis.

Cell image segmentation is an essential task in the field of biomedical image analysis. In recent years, deep learning models, such as U-net, have shown great success in this domain. However, these models often require a large amount of labeled data for training and suffer from a lack of accuracy in segmentation boundaries. In this paper, we propose a novel feedback U-net (F-U-net) architecture to address these challenges. Our model incorporates a feedback mechanism that iteratively refines the initial segmentation masks using information from multiple scales. Additionally, we introduce a novel loss function that encourages accurate segmentation boundaries. We evaluate our approach on multiple datasets and compare it with state-of-the-art methods. The results demonstrate that our F-U-net outperforms existing methods in terms of both boundary accuracy and overall segmentation performance.

Medical image segmentation is a critical task in computer-aided diagnosis and treatment planning. However, obtaining accurate and reliable segmentation results is challenging due to the limited availability of annotated data. In this paper, we propose a generic ensemble-based deep convolutional neural network (CNN) for semi-supervised medical image segmentation. The proposed method leverages both labeled and unlabeled data to improve the segmentation performance. Specifically, we first train multiple CNN models on the labeled data and use them to generate pseudo-labels for the unlabeled data. These pseudo-labels are then used to train additional CNN models, which are combined through an ensemble strategy to obtain the final segmentation result. Experimental results on a publicly available medical image dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method, achieving state-of-the-art performance in terms of segmentation accuracy and robustness. The proposed method has the potential to significantly improve the efficiency and accuracy of medical image segmentation, thereby facilitating clinical decision-making and improving patient outcomes.

This paper presents a novel approach for semi-supervised medical image segmentation using a generic ensemble based deep convolutional neural network. The proposed method combines multiple deep learning models into an ensemble, which allows for improved performance and robustness. The network is trained using labeled as well as unlabeled medical images, leveraging the benefits of both supervised and unsupervised learning. The experimental results demonstrate that the proposed approach outperforms other state-of-the-art techniques for medical image segmentation. The proposed method shows promise in improving the accuracy and efficiency of medical image segmentation, which can have significant benefits in various medical applications.

Real-time video segmentation networks are widely used in various applications such as video editing, augmented reality, and autonomous driving. However, existing evaluation metrics for these networks often focus on accuracy and do not consider the latency, which is crucial for real-time applications. In this paper, we propose a fair latency-aware metric for evaluating real-time video segmentation networks. Our metric takes into account both the accuracy and the latency of the network, providing a comprehensive evaluation of its performance. We conduct experiments on a benchmark dataset and compare our metric with existing metrics. The results show that our metric provides a fair evaluation of the network's performance, considering both accuracy and latency. We believe that our metric can be a valuable tool for researchers and practitioners in the field of real-time video segmentation networks.

Real-time video segmentation networks are widely used in various applications, including augmented reality, object tracking, and video editing. However, existing metrics for evaluating the performance of these networks often focus on accuracy and do not take into account the latency of the system. In this paper, we propose a fair latency-aware metric for real-time video segmentation networks. Our metric considers both the accuracy and latency of the system, providing a more comprehensive evaluation of the network's performance. We evaluate our metric on a benchmark dataset and compare it with existing metrics. The results show that our metric provides a fair and accurate evaluation of the network's performance, taking into account both the accuracy and latency of the system.

This paper presents a novel approach for automating the design of deep learning methods for biomedical image segmentation. The proposed method utilizes a genetic algorithm to search for optimal network architectures and hyperparameters. The algorithm is guided by a fitness function that evaluates the performance of the network on a validation dataset. The approach is demonstrated on two different biomedical image segmentation tasks, achieving state-of-the-art results on both. The results show that the automated design process can effectively discover high-performing deep learning methods for biomedical image segmentation, saving time and effort compared to manual design. The proposed approach has the potential to accelerate the development of deep learning methods for biomedical image analysis.

This paper presents a novel approach for the automated design of deep learning methods for biomedical image segmentation. The traditional manual design of deep learning architectures can be time-consuming and requires expert knowledge. In this work, a genetic algorithm is proposed to automatically search for optimal network architectures and hyperparameters. The algorithm is applied to the task of segmenting biomedical images, specifically retinal images and histopathology images. The results demonstrate that the automated approach can achieve comparable performance to manually-designed networks while significantly reducing the human effort involved. Furthermore, the automated approach is shown to be robust across different datasets and can adapt to various segmentation tasks. Overall, this work shows promising potential in advancing the field of biomedical image segmentation by automating the design process of deep learning methods.

Few-shot segmentation is a challenging task in computer vision that aims to segment objects in images with only a few annotated examples. In this paper, we propose a novel approach called CRNet (Cross-Reference Networks) for few-shot segmentation. CRNet leverages cross-referencing between the support and query images to improve the segmentation performance. Specifically, we introduce a cross-reference module that learns to align the features of the support and query images, enabling effective transfer of knowledge from the support to the query images. We also propose a cross-reference loss function that encourages the network to generate consistent segmentations across different views of the same object. Experimental results on benchmark datasets demonstrate that CRNet outperforms state-of-the-art few-shot segmentation methods, achieving significant improvements in segmentation accuracy. Our approach shows promise for addressing the challenging problem of few-shot segmentation in computer vision.

Few-shot segmentation is a challenging task that requires training models to accurately segment objects from only a few labeled examples. In this paper, we propose a novel approach called CRNet, which leverages cross-reference networks to enhance the performance of few-shot segmentation. The CRNet consists of two main components: a cross-reference module and a segmentation module. The cross-reference module utilizes a cross-reference network to generate cross-references for each pixel in the image, which provides additional contextual information for the segmentation task. The segmentation module then utilizes these cross-references to improve the accuracy of the segmentation. We evaluate the proposed CRNet on several benchmark datasets and compare it with existing state-of-the-art few-shot segmentation methods. The experimental results demonstrate that CRNet achieves superior performance and outperforms existing methods in terms of segmentation accuracy and efficiency. Therefore, CRNet can be considered as a promising solution for few-shot segmentation tasks.

This paper presents a deep learning approach for ranking response surfaces, with a focus on its application to optimal stopping problems. The traditional approach to ranking response surfaces involves fitting a regression model to the data and then using the model to rank the surfaces. However, this approach has limitations in terms of accuracy and scalability. In this paper, we propose a deep learning model that directly ranks the response surfaces without the need for a separate regression model. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through experiments on various datasets and show that it outperforms the traditional approach in terms of accuracy and scalability. Furthermore, we apply our deep learning model to solve optimal stopping problems, which involve making decisions on when to stop a process in order to maximize a certain objective. Our experimental results show that our deep learning model can effectively solve optimal stopping problems and outperforms existing methods. Overall, our work contributes to the field of ranking response surfaces and provides a novel approach for solving optimal stopping problems.

This paper presents a deep learning approach for ranking response surfaces, with a focus on applications to optimal stopping problems. Response surfaces are commonly used in decision-making problems to model the relationship between input variables and a output variable of interest. Traditional methods for ranking response surfaces rely on statistical regression techniques, but these methods may not be able to capture the complex and nonlinear relationships present in many real-world problems. In contrast, deep learning models have demonstrated superior performance in capturing complex patterns and relationships in various domains. In this paper, we propose a deep learning architecture that is specifically tailored for ranking response surfaces. We provide theoretical insights into the performance guarantees of the proposed approach and demonstrate its effectiveness through extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets. We also apply the proposed method to two practical optimal stopping problems and show that it outperforms traditional methods in terms of accuracy and efficiency. Overall, our results suggest that deep learning techniques can be a valuable tool for ranking response surfaces and solving optimal stopping problems.

This paper presents a novel approach to improve the learning effectiveness for object detection and classification in cluttered backgrounds. The proposed method utilizes a combination of deep learning techniques and image processing algorithms to enhance the accuracy and efficiency of object detection and classification tasks. The approach involves pre-processing the input images to remove clutter and enhance the visibility of objects, followed by training a deep neural network to detect and classify the objects. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms existing approaches in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency. The findings of this study have significant implications for various applications, such as autonomous driving, surveillance systems, and robotics.

This paper examines the challenges and proposes a novel approach to improve learning effectiveness for object detection and classification in cluttered backgrounds. Object detection and classification are important tasks in computer vision and have numerous applications such as surveillance, autonomous driving, and robotics. However, in cluttered backgrounds, the presence of irrelevant objects and occlusions can make these tasks more challenging. 

The proposed approach utilizes a deep neural network architecture that integrates object detection and classification modules. The network is trained using a combination of labeled data and weakly labeled data, which is obtained by automatically mining unlabeled images. To handle the challenges posed by cluttered backgrounds, the network incorporates spatial attention mechanisms that allow the network to focus on relevant regions of the image and suppress irrelevant information. 

The experimental results demonstrate that the proposed approach outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods on benchmark datasets for object detection and classification in cluttered backgrounds. The approach achieves higher accuracy and faster execution time, making it a promising solution for practical applications. The findings contribute to the field of computer vision by providing an effective approach for improving learning effectiveness in challenging environments.

This paper presents a novel approach for 3D semi-supervised learning using uncertainty-aware multi-view co-training. The proposed method leverages multiple views of 3D data to improve the performance of semi-supervised learning algorithms. The key idea is to use uncertainty estimates from each view to guide the co-training process, where the most uncertain samples are selected for labeling. The uncertainty estimates are obtained using a deep neural network that is trained to predict the confidence of the model's predictions. Experimental results on several benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method, achieving state-of-the-art performance in 3D semi-supervised learning tasks. The proposed approach has the potential to be applied in various domains, such as computer vision and robotics, where 3D data is prevalent.

3D Semi-Supervised Learning with Uncertainty-Aware Multi-View Co-Training is an academic paper that introduces a new approach for semi-supervised learning in 3D environments. The proposed method combines multiple views of the 3D data and incorporates uncertainty modeling to improve the accuracy of the learning process. By leveraging the complementary information from multiple views, the system can effectively handle the limited labeled data. In addition, the uncertainty modeling helps the system to identify and handle the uncertain or ambiguous samples, further enhancing the learning performance. The paper presents experimental results on various 3D datasets, which demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach in improving the classification accuracy compared to existing methods.

This paper presents a novel approach for maximizing linear-fractional utility in binary classification tasks using calibrated surrogate models. The proposed method aims to address the limitations of existing approaches by incorporating calibration techniques to ensure that the predicted probabilities are well-calibrated. The authors demonstrate the effectiveness of their approach through extensive experiments on various datasets, showing that it outperforms existing methods in terms of utility maximization. The results suggest that calibrated surrogate maximization can significantly improve the performance of binary classification models, making it a promising direction for future research in this field.

This academic paper introduces a novel framework for maximizing linear-fractional utility in binary classification tasks. The proposed approach utilizes a calibrated surrogate model that accurately approximates the true utility function. By calibrating the surrogate using a proper scoring rule, the model is able to accurately estimate the probabilities of the positive class. The authors demonstrate the effectiveness of their approach through extensive experimentation on various datasets, comparing it to several existing methods in terms of utility maximization. The results show that the proposed framework outperforms existing methods and achieves higher utility scores in binary classification tasks.

This paper proposes a novel clustering algorithm called Residual-Sparse Fuzzy $C$-Means (RSFCM) that incorporates morphological reconstruction and wavelet frames. The RSFCM algorithm aims to improve the clustering performance by effectively handling the noise and outliers in the data. The algorithm first applies morphological reconstruction to remove the noise and outliers, and then uses wavelet frames to extract the relevant features from the data. The RSFCM algorithm is evaluated on several benchmark datasets and compared with other clustering algorithms. The results show that the RSFCM algorithm outperforms the other algorithms in terms of clustering accuracy and robustness to noise and outliers. Overall, this paper presents a promising approach for improving the performance of fuzzy $C$-means clustering algorithms by incorporating morphological reconstruction and wavelet frames.

This paper presents a novel clustering algorithm called Residual-Sparse Fuzzy $C$-Means (RSFCM) which incorporates morphological reconstruction and wavelet frames. The proposed algorithm is designed to overcome the limitations of traditional Fuzzy $C$-Means (FCM) algorithms, such as sensitivity to noise and outliers, by using morphological reconstruction to preprocess the data and wavelet frames to capture the complex structures in the data. The RSFCM algorithm is evaluated on several benchmark datasets and compared against other state-of-the-art clustering algorithms. The results show that the RSFCM algorithm outperforms the other algorithms in terms of clustering accuracy and robustness to noise and outliers. Additionally, the RSFCM algorithm is computationally efficient, making it suitable for large-scale clustering tasks. Overall, this paper presents a valuable contribution to the field of clustering algorithms and provides a promising approach for solving complex data clustering problems.

Brain tumor segmentation is a critical task in medical image analysis, as it plays a crucial role in diagnosis and treatment planning. In this paper, we propose a novel one-pass multi-task network with cross-task guided attention for brain tumor segmentation. Our network consists of two branches, one for tumor segmentation and the other for tumor subtype classification. The two branches share a common encoder, which allows for efficient feature extraction. Additionally, we introduce a cross-task guided attention mechanism, which enables the network to focus on relevant regions for both tasks. We evaluate our approach on a publicly available brain tumor dataset and compare it with state-of-the-art methods. The experimental results demonstrate that our proposed network achieves superior performance in both tumor segmentation and subtype classification tasks. Our approach shows promise for improving the accuracy and efficiency of brain tumor analysis in clinical settings.

Brain tumor segmentation is a crucial task in medical imaging that aims to accurately delineate tumor regions, which is important for diagnosis, treatment planning, and monitoring. In this paper, we propose a novel one-pass multi-task network with cross-task guided attention for brain tumor segmentation. Our proposed network architecture combines both deep supervision and multi-task learning approaches to improve the segmentation performance. Furthermore, we introduce a cross-task guided attention mechanism that leverages the inter-task relationships to enhance the segmentation accuracy. We evaluate our approach on a publicly available brain tumor dataset and compare it with several state-of-the-art methods. The experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method, achieving competitive performance in terms of segmentation accuracy and computational efficiency. Overall, our work contributes to the improvement of brain tumor segmentation methods and has potential applications in clinical practice.

Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have shown great potential in generating realistic and high-quality samples. However, training GANs from incomplete observations, where only partial information is available, remains a challenging task. In this paper, we propose a novel approach for training GANs from incomplete observations using factorised discriminators. Our approach leverages the idea of factorising the discriminator into multiple sub-discriminators, each responsible for a specific aspect of the data. We introduce a new training algorithm that alternates between training the generator and updating the sub-discriminators. Experimental results on various datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in generating high-quality samples from incomplete observations. Our approach outperforms existing methods in terms of sample quality and diversity, and shows robustness to different levels of incompleteness in the observations. Overall, our work contributes to the advancement of GANs in handling incomplete observations, opening up new possibilities for applications in various domains.

This paper presents a method to train generative adversarial networks (GANs) when the observations are incomplete. GANs are a powerful deep learning technique that involve training a generator network to produce synthetic data that is indistinguishable from real data, and a discriminator network to distinguish between real and synthetic data. However, when the observations are incomplete, the standard GAN framework struggles to learn meaningful representations. To address this issue, the authors propose a novel approach called Factorised Discriminators. The key idea is to factorise the discriminator network into sub-networks that jointly model different aspects of the incomplete data. The authors demonstrate the effectiveness of their method on various datasets and show that it outperforms existing approaches in terms of both visual quality and quantitative metrics. Overall, the proposed method provides a promising solution for training GANs with incomplete observations, opening up new possibilities for applications in areas such as image inpainting and data imputation.

This paper presents a hierarchical modeling approach for multidimensional data in regularly decomposed spaces. The proposed method utilizes a hierarchical structure to represent the data, allowing for efficient storage and retrieval. The paper discusses the synthesis of the hierarchical model and provides a perspective on its potential applications. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of the approach in handling large-scale multidimensional data. Overall, this paper contributes to the field of data modeling by introducing a hierarchical approach that can be applied to various domains.

This paper presents a hierarchical modeling approach for multidimensional data in regularly decomposed spaces. The proposed method utilizes a hierarchical decomposition of the data space and constructs a multilevel representation of the data. The paper discusses the synthesis of the hierarchical model and provides a perspective on the applications and potential future developments of the approach. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of the hierarchical modeling method in capturing the intrinsic structure of multidimensional data and its potential for various applications. The paper concludes with a discussion on the limitations and challenges of the proposed approach and suggests directions for further research.

This paper presents a method to reduce the model variance of a rectal cancer segmentation network. The proposed method utilizes a combination of data augmentation techniques and model ensemble methods to improve the robustness and generalization of the network. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method significantly reduces the model variance and improves the segmentation accuracy of the network. The findings of this study have important implications for the development of more reliable and accurate rectal cancer segmentation networks.

This paper introduces a method to reduce the model variance of a rectal cancer segmentation network. The segmentation network is trained on a large dataset of rectal cancer images, but it suffers from high variance, resulting in inconsistent segmentation results. To reduce this variance, we propose a novel training strategy that includes multiple steps. First, data augmentation is used to increase the size and diversity of the training set. Second, a regularization technique is applied to encourage feature reuse and prevent overfitting. Third, an ensemble approach is employed to combine the predictions of multiple models trained with different initializations. Experimental results on a publicly available dataset demonstrate that our proposed method significantly reduces the variance of the segmentation network, leading to more consistent and accurate segmentation results.

This paper presents a novel approach for image segmentation using Eikonal region-based active contours. The proposed method combines the advantages of both region-based and active contour models to achieve accurate and efficient segmentation results. The Eikonal equation is used to compute the distance map of the image, which is then used to initialize the active contour. The active contour is iteratively updated using a region-based energy functional that incorporates both local and global information. Experimental results on various benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in terms of segmentation accuracy and computational efficiency. The proposed method outperforms several state-of-the-art segmentation algorithms and shows promising potential for various applications in computer vision and medical imaging.

This paper proposes a new algorithm for image segmentation, called Eikonal Region-based Active Contours (ERAC). Traditional active contour models rely on the geodesic distance of an evolving curve to detect the boundaries of an object in an image. However, these models often lack robustness and struggle with complex image structures. The ERAC approach addresses these limitations by adopting the Eikonal region concept, which considers regional information when evolving contours. The algorithm uses the fast marching method to compute the geodesic distance and incorporates a region term that penalizes movement away from the object boundaries. Experimental results demonstrate that ERAC outperforms existing active contour models in terms of accuracy and efficiency, particularly in challenging scenarios such as images with intensity inhomogeneity and noise. Therefore, ERAC shows great potential for various applications, including medical image segmentation and object tracking.

This paper proposes a novel approach for end-to-end training of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) with Conditional Random Fields (CRFs) using differentiable dual-decomposition. The authors introduce a new energy function that combines the CNN and CRF potentials, and develop a differentiable dual-decomposition algorithm to optimize this energy function. They demonstrate the effectiveness of their approach on various computer vision tasks, including image segmentation and object recognition, achieving state-of-the-art performance. The proposed method allows for joint training of CNNs and CRFs, eliminating the need for separate training and inference steps, and enabling end-to-end optimization. The experimental results validate the superiority of the proposed approach over existing methods, highlighting its potential for advancing the field of computer vision.

In recent years, convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have achieved remarkable success in various computer vision tasks. However, CNNs are limited in their ability to capture long-range dependencies and perform structured prediction tasks. Conditional random fields (CRFs) have been used to model higher-order dependencies and improve performance in such tasks, but the traditional approach of training CNN-CRF models is time-consuming and requires extensive manual tuning. In this paper, we propose an end-to-end training approach for CNN-CRF models using differentiable dual-decomposition, which allows for efficient training and automatic parameter tuning. Our experiments on several benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms traditional approaches in terms of accuracy and efficiency, making it a promising technique for structured prediction tasks in computer vision.

Medical image segmentation is a crucial task in medical image analysis, as it plays a vital role in diagnosis and treatment planning. In this paper, we propose a novel approach for medical image segmentation using hierarchical attention networks. Our method leverages the hierarchical structure of medical images to capture both local and global contextual information. We introduce a hierarchical attention mechanism that dynamically assigns weights to different image regions based on their importance for segmentation. Experimental results on a publicly available medical image dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, achieving state-of-the-art performance in terms of segmentation accuracy. Our proposed method has the potential to improve the accuracy and efficiency of medical image segmentation, thereby benefiting clinical practice and patient care.

Medical image segmentation is an essential task for several clinical applications. In this paper, we propose a novel hierarchical attention network (HAN) framework for medical image segmentation. Our HAN model incorporates both local and global contextual information, allowing it to capture finer details and larger structures simultaneously. We evaluate the performance of our model on two publicly available medical imaging datasets: the BraTS 2018 dataset for brain tumor segmentation and the ISIC 2018 dataset for skin lesion segmentation. Experimental results demonstrate that our HAN model achieves state-of-the-art segmentation performance on both datasets. Furthermore, we conduct extensive ablation studies to analyze the effectiveness of different components of our HAN framework. Overall, our proposed HAN model shows promising results and potential for improving medical image segmentation tasks.

Automated weed detection in aerial imagery is an important task in precision agriculture, as it can help farmers identify and manage weed infestations more effectively. In this paper, we propose a novel approach for automated weed detection in aerial imagery that takes into account the context of the surrounding vegetation. We first segment the aerial imagery into different regions based on color and texture features. Then, we extract features from each region and train a deep learning model to classify them as either weed or non-weed. To incorporate context information, we use a graph-based approach to model the relationships between the different regions. Experimental results on a large dataset of aerial imagery demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, achieving high accuracy in weed detection. Our approach has the potential to significantly improve weed management practices in precision agriculture.

Automated weed detection in aerial imagery has gained significant attention in recent years due to the need for efficient and accurate methods for weed management in agricultural fields. In this paper, we propose a novel approach for weed detection using aerial imagery that incorporates contextual information. The proposed method utilizes a deep learning-based approach combined with spatially aware features to improve the accuracy of weed detection. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in accurately detecting weeds in different field conditions. Our method outperforms existing approaches in terms of accuracy and efficiency, making it a valuable tool for weed management in agriculture. Overall, our work contributes to the advancement of automated weed detection techniques and provides a useful framework for future research in this area.

Medical image segmentation is a crucial task in computer-aided diagnosis and treatment planning. However, obtaining accurate segmentation masks for medical images is challenging due to the limited availability of annotated data. In this paper, we propose a semi-supervised approach for medical image segmentation that leverages both labeled and unlabeled data. Our method learns consistency under transformations by training a segmentation network to produce consistent segmentations when the input image is transformed. We introduce a novel consistency loss function that encourages the network to produce similar segmentations for transformed images. We evaluate our approach on two publicly available medical image segmentation datasets and demonstrate that it outperforms state-of-the-art semi-supervised methods. Our method achieves competitive performance even with a small amount of labeled data, making it a promising approach for medical image segmentation in scenarios with limited annotated data.

Medical image segmentation plays a critical role in clinical practice and medical research. However, obtaining labeled training data for supervised segmentation models is often challenging and time-consuming. In this paper, we propose a novel semi-supervised approach for medical image segmentation that leverages the consistency under transformations. Specifically, we utilize a small amount of labeled data along with a large amount of unlabeled data to train a segmentation model. The key idea is to encourage the model to produce consistent segmentations under different transformations applied to the input images. We achieve this by introducing transformations to both the labeled and unlabeled images during training, and enforcing consistency between the segmentations produced by the model on the transformed images. Experimental results on two well-known medical image datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, achieving competitive performance compared to fully supervised methods while requiring significantly fewer labeled data for training.

This paper presents a novel unsupervised video object segmentation method called Anchor Diffusion. The proposed method leverages the temporal coherence of video frames to improve the accuracy of object segmentation. It introduces the concept of anchor frames, which are selected based on their visual similarity to the target frame. These anchor frames are then used to propagate object masks across frames using a diffusion process. Experimental results on benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in terms of segmentation accuracy and temporal consistency. The paper also provides an analysis of the computational efficiency of the proposed method, showing that it is computationally efficient and scalable to large-scale video datasets. Overall, Anchor Diffusion offers a promising approach for unsupervised video object segmentation.

This paper proposes a novel approach for unsupervised video object segmentation based on anchor diffusion. By utilizing anchor points that represent object centers, the proposed method effectively addresses challenges including occlusion, motion blur, and appearance change in video sequences. The anchor points are iteratively displaced and propagated to neighboring regions, leading to the segmentation of objects. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed anchor diffusion method on multiple video datasets, outperforming state-of-the-art unsupervised video object segmentation techniques. The proposed approach provides a promising solution for accurately segmenting objects in videos without requiring any manual annotations.

This paper presents a novel approach for few-shot segmentation of volumetric images using a technique called "squeeze and excite". The proposed method leverages the power of deep neural networks to learn representations from a small number of annotated samples. The squeeze and excite mechanism is used to enhance the discriminative power of the learned features by adaptively recalibrating them.
