Image segmentation is a widely used technique in the field of computer vision for identifying and separating objects in an image. This paper presents a novel approach for image segmentation based on an adaptive distance metric derived from an Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm. The proposed method aims to overcome the limitations of traditional distance-based segmentation techniques by adapting the distance metric dynamically during the segmentation process. Experimental results on various benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of the proposed method in accurately segmenting images with complex structures and varying textures. The adaptive distance-based approach achieves superior performance compared to state-of-the-art segmentation methods, highlighting its potential for various applications in computer vision and image processing.

This paper proposes a novel approach for image segmentation and shape inpainting using a curvature prior in a Markov Random Field (MRF) framework. The authors argue that incorporating curvature information can improve the accuracy and quality of segmentation and inpainting results. They introduce a new energy function that combines the traditional MRF energy with a curvature term, which encourages smooth and coherent boundaries. The proposed method is evaluated on various datasets and compared with existing approaches, demonstrating its effectiveness in achieving accurate and visually pleasing segmentation and inpainting results. The results suggest that the curvature prior can be a valuable tool in MRF-based image processing tasks.

In this paper, we propose a novel approach for segmentation and shape inpainting using a curvature prior based on Markov random fields (MRFs). Traditional segmentation and inpainting methods often suffer from artifacts and inaccuracies due to the lack of explicit shape constraints. Our proposed method overcomes this limitation by incorporating a curvature prior into the energy function of the MRF model. We show that the curvature prior encourages smoother and more accurate segmentations, as well as more realistic and coherent shape inpainting results. We evaluate our method on several benchmark datasets and demonstrate its superiority over state-of-the-art methods in terms of segmentation and inpainting accuracy. Overall, our approach provides a promising solution for solving the challenging tasks of segmentation and shape inpainting.

This paper presents a novel approach for selective image super-resolution, which aims to enhance the resolution of specific regions of an image while preserving the overall image quality. The proposed method utilizes a deep convolutional neural network to learn the mapping between low-resolution and high-resolution image patches. To achieve selective super-resolution, a saliency map is generated to identify the regions of interest in the low-resolution image. The network is then trained to focus on these regions during the super-resolution process. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms existing super-resolution techniques in terms of both objective and subjective image quality measures. The selective super-resolution approach has potential applications in various domains, such as medical imaging, surveillance, and digital photography.

In this paper, we propose a novel approach for selective image super-resolution, which aims to enhance the resolution of specific regions of interest in an image while leaving the rest of the image unchanged. Our method combines convolutional neural networks with a new attention mechanism that allows the network to selectively focus on different regions of the image. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on a diverse range of images and show that it outperforms existing methods in terms of both subjective and objective evaluations. We also provide insights into the inner workings of our network through visualizations and analysis of the attention maps. Overall, our proposed method provides a promising solution for selective image super-resolution, with applications in various fields such as medical imaging and surveillance.

This paper presents a new approach to lung image segmentation using the fuzzy possibilistic C-means (FPCM) algorithm. Lung image segmentation is an important task in medical image analysis, as it plays a crucial role in the diagnosis and treatment of lung diseases. The proposed approach combines the advantages of both fuzzy clustering and possibilistic clustering, allowing for more accurate and robust segmentation results. The FPCM algorithm is modified to incorporate spatial information, which helps to preserve the shape and boundaries of lung structures. Experimental results on a dataset of lung CT images demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach, with improved segmentation accuracy compared to existing methods. The proposed approach has the potential to contribute to the development of computer-aided diagnosis systems for lung diseases.

This paper presents a new approach to lung image segmentation using the fuzzy possibilistic C-means (FPCM) algorithm. The proposed method utilizes the FPCM algorithm to accurately and efficiently classify lung tissues in medical images. The FPCM algorithm incorporates both fuzzy and possibilistic membership functions to handle uncertainties in the data, enabling it to better handle noise and intensity variations in lung images. Experimental results on a dataset of lung images demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms other segmentation algorithms in terms of accuracy, robustness, and computational efficiency. The proposed approach has the potential to improve the accuracy of lung image segmentation, thereby aiding in the diagnosis and treatment of lung diseases.

This paper presents a novel approach for image segmentation using maximin affinity learning. Image segmentation is a fundamental task in computer vision, and it involves partitioning an image into meaningful regions. Traditional methods for image segmentation often rely on handcrafted features or heuristics, which may not generalize well to different types of images. In this paper, we propose a new framework that learns the affinity matrix for image segmentation using a maximin objective function. The proposed method leverages the power of deep learning to automatically learn discriminative features from the input images. Experimental results on benchmark datasets demonstrate that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance in terms of segmentation accuracy and computational efficiency. Furthermore, we conduct extensive ablation studies to analyze the effectiveness of different components in our method. Overall, our work contributes to the field of image segmentation by introducing a novel learning framework that combines deep learning and maximin affinity learning.

Maximin affinity learning is a popular approach in image segmentation where pixel affinities are learned to capture object boundaries. This paper proposes maximin affinity learning for image segmentation using a novel algorithm called the Maximin Affinity Learning of Image Segmentation (MALIS). MALIS is designed to automatically learn pixel affinities based on a deep neural network and exploit these affinities to generate high-quality object segmentations. The paper presents extensive experiments on various datasets to demonstrate the effectiveness of MALIS compared to existing methods. The results show that MALIS achieves state-of-the-art performance on image segmentation tasks, highlighting its potential for practical applications in computer vision and related fields.

This paper presents a novel method for determining lambda-connectedness in image segmentation. Lambda-connectedness is a measure of the connectivity between pixels in an image, and is an important factor in determining the accuracy of image segmentation algorithms. The proposed method utilizes a graph-based approach, where the image is represented as a graph and lambda-connectedness is determined by analyzing the connectivity between nodes. Experimental results on various image datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in accurately determining lambda-connectedness. The proposed method has the potential to improve the performance of image segmentation algorithms and contribute to advancements in computer vision and image processing.

Image segmentation is an important task in computer vision that involves partitioning an image into meaningful regions or objects. Many existing segmentation methods rely on the concept of lambda-connectedness, which characterizes the strength of the connectivity between neighboring pixels. This paper presents a novel approach for lambda-connectedness determination in image segmentation. We propose a graph-based representation of an image, where each pixel is represented as a node and the connectivity between pixels is represented as edges. We then define a metric for lambda-connectedness based on the properties of the graph, such as edge weights and node degrees. To determine the lambda-connectedness of a given set of pixels, we employ graph algorithms such as breadth-first search and Dijkstra's algorithm. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in accurately segmenting images and outperforming state-of-the-art segmentation methods. This paper contributes to the field of image segmentation by providing a robust and efficient technique for lambda-connectedness determination.

This paper presents a study on the effectiveness of a random-detector-efficiency countermeasure in a commercial system. The countermeasure is designed to protect against attacks by randomly varying the efficiency of detectors. The authors conducted experiments to test the effectiveness of this countermeasure and found that it can be easily broken due to an unrealistic assumption made in its design. The results highlight the importance of considering realistic assumptions when designing countermeasures for commercial systems. The findings of this study have implications for the development of more robust and secure countermeasures in the future.

This paper investigates the effectiveness of a countermeasure known as random-detector-efficiency (RDE) in a commercial system. RDE relies on the assumption that the attacker does not have prior knowledge of which detectors are functioning properly. However, our findings reveal that this assumption is easily breakable, rendering RDE ineffective. We propose alternative countermeasures that do not rely on this unrealistic assumption to improve security in commercial systems.

Answer set programming (ASP) is a popular declarative programming paradigm for solving combinatorial problems. In ASP, a program consists of rules that define the relationships between variables and constraints on their values. Answer sets, or stable models, are the solutions to these programs. In this paper, we introduce the concept of cascade products of answer set programs, which allows for the composition of multiple programs into a single program. We provide a formal definition of cascade products and present algorithms for computing them. We also discuss the properties of cascade products and their applications in solving complex combinatorial problems. Our experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of cascade products in improving the efficiency and scalability of ASP solvers. Overall, this paper contributes to the understanding and advancement of answer set programming by introducing a new technique for program composition.

Answer Set Programming (ASP) is a widely used approach in Knowledge Representation and Reasoning, where a reasoning engine is used to compute answer sets for a given logic program. In this paper, we introduce the concept of cascade products for ASP programs, which are formed by combining multiple programs and taking the union of their answer sets. We develop a framework for reasoning with cascade products, and present the necessary definitions and algorithms. Additionally, we demonstrate the benefits of cascade products in practical applications, showing their usefulness for solving complex problems with large-scale datasets. Our experimental results indicate that cascade products can significantly improve the performance of ASP systems, making them more scalable and efficient for real-world scenarios. Overall, this paper provides a comprehensive study and analysis of cascade products in the context of Answer Set Programming, offering insights and practical guidelines for their effective utilization.

The abstract for the academic paper titled "Phase Diagram of Metal-Insulator Transition in System with Anderson-Hubbard Centers" discusses the phase diagram of a system with Anderson-Hubbard centers, which is a model for the metal-insulator transition. The authors use a combination of numerical and analytical techniques to study the phase diagram and identify the different phases that occur as a function of temperature and interaction strength. They find that the system exhibits a metal-insulator transition at a critical interaction strength, and that the transition is accompanied by the formation of a Mott gap. The authors also investigate the effect of disorder on the phase diagram and find that disorder can suppress the metal-insulator transition. Overall, this study provides valuable insights into the metal-insulator transition in systems with Anderson-Hubbard centers and highlights the importance of disorder in determining the phase diagram.

The paper investigates the phase diagram of a system with Anderson-Hubbard centers. The study aims to better understand the metal-insulator transition in these systems. The authors use a combination of numerical calculations and analytical methods to determine the critical points and regions of the phase diagram. They find that the system exhibits a rich phase space, with a phase transition between metallic and insulating phases. The findings of this paper contribute to the understanding of metal-insulator transitions and have potential implications for the design of new materials with desired electronic properties.

This paper introduces a novel approach to unsupervised learning using mixtures of skewed distributions with hypercube contours. The proposed method aims to capture complex data distributions by modeling them as a combination of skewed distributions. The hypercube contours are used to define the boundaries of each distribution, allowing for a more flexible and accurate representation of the data. The paper presents the mathematical formulation of the proposed method and provides experimental results on various datasets to demonstrate its effectiveness. The results show that the proposed approach outperforms existing unsupervised learning methods in terms of clustering accuracy and data representation. Overall, this paper contributes to the field of unsupervised learning by introducing a new approach that can effectively model complex data distributions.

The paper presents a novel approach for unsupervised learning using mixtures of skewed distributions with hypercube contours. The proposed method combines a mixture model framework with skewed distributions to capture complex data structures with irregular shapes, such as clusters with different orientations or elongated shapes. The hypercube contours are used to define the boundaries of each cluster, allowing for accurate clustering of data points. Experimental results on various datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and superiority of the proposed method compared to other state-of-the-art approaches. The findings of this study contribute to the field of unsupervised learning by providing a robust and flexible approach for modeling and clustering complex data structures.

The paper "Paradoxical signaling regulates structural plasticity in dendritic spines" investigates the role of paradoxical signaling in the regulation of structural plasticity in dendritic spines. The authors demonstrate that paradoxical signaling, characterized by the activation of both inhibitory and excitatory pathways, is necessary for the induction of spine enlargement and subsequent stabilization. They further show that this paradoxical signaling is mediated by the activation of specific molecular pathways, including the activation of protein kinase A and the inhibition of protein phosphatase 1. These findings provide new insights into the mechanisms underlying dendritic spine plasticity and highlight the importance of paradoxical signaling in this process.

The abstract of the academic paper "Paradoxical signaling regulates structural plasticity in dendritic spines" describes the research conducted on the role of paradoxical signaling in the regulation of structural plasticity in dendritic spines. The study used two-photon microscopy to visualize and measure changes in dendritic spine morphology in response to different signaling pathways. The results showed that paradoxical signaling, characterized by simultaneous activation of both inhibitory and excitatory signaling pathways, is crucial for maintaining a balance between spine stability and plasticity. This paradoxical signaling was found to be mediated by a specific protein complex, leading to changes in spine shape and size. Overall, the findings highlight the importance of paradoxical signaling in regulating structural plasticity in dendritic spines and provide insights into the underlying molecular mechanisms involved.

Magnetic reconnection is a fundamental process in plasma physics that occurs in various astrophysical and laboratory settings. It is known to generate high-energy particles through the acceleration of ions. In this paper, we investigate the effect of large-scale effective potentials on ion heating during magnetic reconnection. We find that these potentials can significantly reduce ion heating by suppressing the acceleration of ions. Our results suggest that the presence of large-scale effective potentials can have important implications for understanding the dynamics of magnetic reconnection and the generation of high-energy particles in astrophysical and laboratory plasmas.

Magnetic reconnection is a fundamental process in plasma physics that often leads to the heating of ions and the generation of energetic particles. In this paper, we propose a novel method to reduce ion heating during magnetic reconnection by imposing large-scale effective potentials. We demonstrate through simulations that these potentials can effectively trap ions and prevent them from gaining excessive energy during the reconnection process. This reduction in ion heating has important implications for various astrophysical and laboratory plasmas, as it can help explain the observed temperature profiles and particle distributions. Our findings provide a new perspective on the role of large-scale potentials in magnetic reconnection and open up new possibilities for controlling plasma heating in various applications.

This paper explores the application of Keplerian dynamics on the Heisenberg group and other mathematical spaces. The Heisenberg group is a non-commutative Lie group that arises in quantum mechanics and has been studied extensively in recent years. The authors investigate the behavior of Keplerian orbits on the Heisenberg group and compare it to the classical case on Euclidean spaces. They also explore the possibility of extending these dynamics to other mathematical spaces, such as Riemannian manifolds and symplectic manifolds. The results provide insights into the interplay between classical and quantum mechanics and open up new avenues for further research in this area.

This academic paper explores Keplerian dynamics in different mathematical settings, with a special focus on the Heisenberg group. The Heisenberg group is a non-commutative extension of Euclidean space widely used in the study of quantum mechanics. The paper presents a detailed analysis of Keplerian motions on the Heisenberg group, including the derivation of the equations of motion and the characterization of orbits. Furthermore, the paper discusses similar dynamics in other mathematical settings, such as Lie groups and Riemannian manifolds, providing comparisons and connections to the Heisenberg group case. The results obtained contribute to a deeper understanding of Keplerian dynamics in diverse mathematical contexts and can potentially find applications in various fields, including physics and control theory.

This paper presents analytic expressions for stochastic distances between relaxed complex Wishart distributions. The relaxed complex Wishart distribution is a generalization of the complex Wishart distribution, which is commonly used in multivariate statistics. The stochastic distances between these distributions are important for various applications, such as hypothesis testing and model selection. However, computing these distances can be computationally expensive. In this paper, we derive closed-form expressions for the stochastic distances between relaxed complex Wishart distributions, which significantly reduce the computational burden. We validate our results through numerical experiments and demonstrate the usefulness of the derived expressions in practical scenarios. Overall, this paper provides a valuable contribution to the field of multivariate statistics by providing efficient and accurate methods for computing stochastic distances between relaxed complex Wishart distributions.

The paper introduces a new method for calculating stochastic distances between relaxed complex Wishart distributions. These distances are of interest in many applications, including statistical inference and machine learning. The authors derive analytic expressions for these distances, allowing for efficient computation and comparison. The accuracy of the derived expressions is demonstrated through numerical experiments. The proposed method offers a valuable tool for analyzing and comparing relaxed complex Wishart distributions in various research domains.

This paper investigates the global existence and asymptotic behavior of solutions to a chemotaxis-fluid system on a general bounded domain. The chemotaxis-fluid system is a mathematical model that describes the interaction between a fluid flow and the movement of cells in response to chemical signals. The authors prove the global existence of solutions to the system using a combination of energy estimates and compactness arguments. They also study the long-time behavior of the solutions and show that they converge to a steady state as time goes to infinity. The results of this paper provide a better understanding of the dynamics of the chemotaxis-fluid system and have potential applications in various fields such as biology and medicine.

This paper investigates the global existence and asymptotic behavior of solutions to a chemotaxis-fluid system on a general bounded domain. The system consists of a fluid equations coupled with a chemotaxis equation, which describes the movement of cells in response to a chemical gradient. By utilizing the method of energy estimates, the authors prove the global existence of solutions to the system. Furthermore, they establish the existence of a global attractor, which characterizes the long-term behavior of the solutions. The paper also discusses the asymptotic behavior of the solutions as time approaches infinity, providing insights into the dynamics of the system. These results contribute to the understanding of chemotaxis-fluid systems and can be applied to diverse fields such as biology and medicine.

This paper investigates the phenomenon of Anderson localization in a partially random Bragg grating. The authors propose a conserved area theorem to explain the localization of light in this system. They use numerical simulations to demonstrate the validity of their theorem and compare their results with experimental data. The findings of this study provide insights into the behavior of light in disordered photonic structures and contribute to the understanding of Anderson localization in complex systems.

The paper investigates Anderson localization in a partially random Bragg grating and the existence of a conserved area theorem. The researchers numerically analyze the propagation of light through the grating and identify the conditions under which Anderson localization occurs. They also propose a conserved area theorem based on the symmetry properties of the system. The results contribute to the understanding of Anderson localization in complex optical systems and provide insights into the design and control of light propagation in photonic structures.

In this paper, we investigate the approximation of quantum gates using lattices. We propose a novel method for approximating quantum gates by representing them as lattices and applying lattice-based algorithms. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by comparing the approximation results with existing methods. Our findings show that the lattice-based approximation method achieves comparable accuracy while reducing computational complexity. This research contributes to the field of quantum computing by providing a new perspective on gate approximation techniques and offering a potential avenue for improving the efficiency of quantum algorithms.

Quantum gates are a fundamental building block in quantum computing, used to manipulate qubits and perform computations. However, implementing these gates in physical systems can be challenging due to various practical limitations. In this paper, we propose a new approach for approximating quantum gates using lattices. We first provide a mathematical framework for representing quantum gates as lattices and derive a set of conditions for their approximation. We then present a novel algorithm for constructing lattice-based approximations of quantum gates. Our algorithm utilizes the structure of lattices to efficiently generate gate approximations with high accuracy. We evaluate the performance of our approach using numerical simulations and compare it with existing methods. The results demonstrate that our lattice-based approximation technique outperforms current state-of-the-art methods in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency. Our findings have implications for the design and implementation of quantum computing technologies.

This paper presents an analytic approach to the problem of matroid representability, specifically focusing on the cardinality of sets of k-independent vectors over finite fields. The authors introduce a new method for analyzing the maximum distance separable conjecture, which is a well-known open problem in the field. The paper provides theoretical results and computational experiments to support their approach. The findings suggest that the analytic approach can provide valuable insights into the problem of matroid representability and contribute to the understanding of the maximum distance separable conjecture.

This paper provides a note on an analytic approach to the problem of matroid representability, specifically focusing on the cardinality of sets of k-independent vectors over finite fields and the Maximum Distance Separable (MDS) conjecture. The MDS conjecture is a well-known open problem in coding theory, which states that a linear error-correcting code over a finite field is MDS if and only if its minimum distance exceeds a certain threshold. The paper applies an analytic approach to study the cardinality of k-independent vectors in matroids, and their relation to the MDS conjecture. The authors present theoretical results and provide computational examples to support their findings. This note contributes to the ongoing research on matroid representability and the MDS conjecture, and suggests possible directions for further investigation.

This paper presents the experiment simulation configurations used in the Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (DUNE) Conceptual Design Report (CDR). DUNE is a next-generation neutrino experiment that aims to study neutrino oscillations and other neutrino properties. The simulation configurations include the detector geometry, materials, and physics processes used to model the interactions of neutrinos and other particles in the DUNE detectors. The paper describes the simulation tools and software used, as well as the validation and benchmarking of the simulation configurations. The results of the simulations are compared to data from previous experiments and used to inform the design and optimization of the DUNE detectors. The paper concludes with a discussion of the future directions and improvements for the simulation configurations in DUNE.

This paper presents the experiment simulation configurations used in the Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (DUNE) Conceptual Design Report (CDR). DUNE is a long-baseline neutrino oscillation experiment aimed at studying the properties of neutrinos and searching for CP (Charge-Parity) violation in the neutrino sector. The paper discusses the various aspects of the experiment simulations, including the beam simulation, detector simulation, and event reconstruction. It also describes the software tools and frameworks used for the simulations, such as Geant4 and LArSoft. This paper presents a theoretical and experimental study of non-diffracting chirped Bessel waves in optical antiguides. The authors investigate the propagation characteristics of these waves in antiguides with different refractive index profiles. The results show that the chirped Bessel waves can maintain their non-diffracting properties over a certain distance, which is determined by the chirp rate and the refractive index profile. The authors also demonstrate the generation and manipulation of these waves using a spatial light modulator. The findings of this study have potential applications in optical communication and imaging systems.

In this paper, we investigate the generation and properties of non-diffracting chirped Bessel waves in optical antiguides. We demonstrate that by properly designing the waveguide structure and applying a chirp term to the Bessel function, non-diffracting Bessel waves can be achieved over a wide range of propagation distances. We further analyze the impact of different parameters on the propagation and focusing properties of these waves. Our findings show the potential of using non-diffracting chirped Bessel waves in various applications, such as optical trapping, particle manipulation, and beam shaping. These results provide important insights for the design and optimization of waveguide devices utilizing non-diffracting Bessel waves.

This paper explores the concept of subgaussian sequences in probability and Fourier analysis. Subgaussian sequences are defined as sequences of random variables that have tails that decay faster than those of a Gaussian distribution. The paper discusses the properties and applications of subgaussian sequences in various areas of probability theory and Fourier analysis, including concentration inequalities, empirical processes, and random matrices. The authors provide a comprehensive overview of the theory and techniques related to subgaussian sequences, and present several key results and open problems in the field. Overall, this paper serves as a valuable resource for researchers and practitioners interested in the study of subgaussian sequences and their applications in probability and Fourier analysis.

In this paper, we provide a comprehensive overview of subgaussian sequences and their applications in probability and Fourier analysis. Subgaussian sequences are a class of random variables that have tails that decay at least as fast as a Gaussian distribution. We discuss various properties and characterizations of subgaussian sequences, including concentration inequalities and moment inequalities. We also explore the connection between subgaussian sequences and concentration of measure phenomena. Furthermore, we examine the role of subgaussian sequences in Fourier analysis, including their use in estimating the power spectrum of a stationary time series. Finally, we discuss some open problems and future directions in the study of subgaussian sequences. Overall, this paper provides a comprehensive treatment of subgaussian sequences and highlights their importance in various areas of probability and Fourier analysis.

In this paper, we investigate the asymptotic behavior of a partition function related to the sinh-model. We derive an asymptotic expansion for the partition function and analyze its properties. We show that the expansion is valid in a certain parameter regime and discuss the implications of this result. Our findings provide insights into the behavior of the sinh-model and contribute to the understanding of its thermodynamic properties.

The partition function of the sinh-model plays a crucial role in understanding the behavior of quantum systems. In this paper, we study the asymptotic expansion of this partition function for large values of the parameter. We use the method of steepest descent to derive the leading-order term of the expansion. We then calculate the next-to-leading order terms using techniques from complex analysis. Our results provide insights into the behavior of the sinh-model and have potential applications in various areas of physics.

This paper presents a series of experiments conducted to increase the used energy with the PEGASUS railgun. The railgun is a type of electromagnetic launcher that uses magnetic fields to accelerate projectiles to high velocities. The goal of this research is to optimize the energy transfer efficiency of the railgun system. The experiments involve varying parameters such as projectile mass, rail length, and magnetic field strength to determine their effects on energy transfer. The results show that increasing the projectile mass and rail length leads to higher energy transfer, while increasing the magnetic field strength has a more complex effect. These findings provide valuable insights for improving the performance of railgun systems and can contribute to the development of more efficient and powerful electromagnetic launchers.

This academic paper presents a series of experiments aimed at increasing the used energy in a PEGASUS railgun system. Railguns are electromagnetic launchers that utilize magnetic fields to propel projectiles at high velocities. This paper provides a comprehensive study of log-symplectic manifolds, which are a class of symplectic manifolds with additional logarithmic structures. This paper explores the Kac-Moody extensions of 3-algebras and their relevance to M2-branes. The authors introduce the concept of a 3-algebra and discuss its properties and applications in physics. This paper investigates the role of Kac-Moody extensions in the context of 3-algebras and M2-branes. 3-algebras are a natural generalization of Lie algebras and are closely related to M-theory, a 11-dimensional theory of gravity. The authors introduce a new class of 3-algebras called Kac-Moody extensions and study their properties. They show that these extensions can be used to describe the dynamics of M2-branes in certain backgrounds. In this paper, we study the existence of positive Ricci curvature on simply-connected manifolds with cohomogeneity-two torus actions. We provide a classification of such manifolds and show that under certain conditions, they admit metrics with positive Ricci curvature. Our results extend previous work on positive Ricci curvature and provide new insights into the geometry of torus actions on manifolds.

This paper investigates the existence and properties of simply-connected manifolds with cohomogeneity-two torus actions that have positive Ricci curvature. The authors provide examples of such manifolds and explore their geometric properties. They also study the differentiable structure and topological properties of these manifolds.
