This paper explores the concept of d-complete posets as a generalization of Young diagrams for the Jeu de Taquin property. The Jeu de Taquin property is a combinatorial property of Young diagrams that allows for the rearrangement of cells in a specific manner. The authors introduce the notion of d-complete posets, which are posets that satisfy certain conditions related to the Jeu de Taquin property. They provide a characterization of d-complete posets and study their properties. The authors also establish a connection between d-complete posets and Young diagrams, showing that d-complete posets can be used to encode the Jeu de Taquin property. This paper contributes to the understanding of the Jeu de Taquin property and provides a new perspective on its generalization through d-complete posets.

This paper presents a new generalization of Young diagrams for the Jeu de Taquin property using d-complete posets. The Jeu de Taquin property refers to a property exhibited by Young diagrams where one can move cells along certain paths while preserving their shape. Traditionally, Young diagrams have been used to study this property, but they have limitations in terms of their shape. In this paper, the authors introduce d-complete posets as a new way to generalize Young diagrams for the Jeu de Taquin property. They define the concept of d-completeness and provide a set of axioms that a poset must satisfy to be considered d-complete. Furthermore, the authors show that d-complete posets can be used to model various combinatorial objects and study their properties. Finally, they demonstrate how d-complete posets generalize the Jeu de Taquin property and provide examples of their application in solving combinatorial problems. Overall, this paper contributes to the understanding and application of d-complete posets in the context of the Jeu de Taquin property and provides a new perspective on the study of Young diagrams.

This paper presents a novel approach for estimating gaze direction using full-face appearance-based methods. Traditional gaze estimation methods rely on eye tracking, which can be intrusive and limited in accuracy. In contrast, our approach utilizes a deep neural network to analyze facial features and estimate gaze direction. We propose a multi-task learning framework that simultaneously predicts head pose and gaze direction, leveraging the correlation between these two tasks. Our experiments on a large-scale dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, achieving state-of-the-art performance in gaze estimation. Furthermore, we conduct extensive ablation studies to analyze the impact of different components in our model. Overall, our work contributes to the field of gaze estimation by providing a non-intrusive and accurate method that can be applied in various real-world scenarios.

The abstract of the paper "It's Written All Over Your Face: Full-Face Appearance-Based Gaze Estimation" discusses a novel method for estimating gaze direction using full-face appearance information. The authors propose a deep learning-based approach that takes advantage of the entire face image to improve accuracy in gaze estimation. They collected a large-scale dataset of faces with annotated gaze directions to train and test their model. The results show that their method outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in both accuracy and robustness. The authors also provide qualitative analysis of their model's performance and discuss potential applications of full-face appearance-based gaze estimation in various fields. Overall, the paper presents a significant advancement in gaze estimation using facial appearance information.

In this paper, we investigate the phase diagram of the zero-bandwidth extended Hubbard model with intersite magnetic interactions in the strong on-site repulsion limit. We use a combination of mean-field theory and numerical simulations to study the ground state properties of the model. We find that the phase diagram exhibits a rich variety of phases, including antiferromagnetic, ferromagnetic, and paramagnetic phases. We also analyze the effect of the intersite magnetic interactions on the phase diagram and find that they can induce additional phases and modify the boundaries between different phases. Our results provide insights into the behavior of strongly correlated electron systems with intersite magnetic interactions and have implications for the understanding of magnetic ordering in real materials.

The paper presents a phase diagram of the zero-bandwidth extended Hubbard model with intersite magnetic interactions in the strong on-site repulsion limit. The model is studied using the Gutzwiller mean field approximation and Monte Carlo simulations. The phase diagram is found to exhibit a variety of phases including a Mott insulating phase, a ferromagnetic phase, a charge-density-wave phase, and a coexistence phase. The effects of the intersite magnetic interactions on the phase diagram are analyzed and discussed. The findings provide valuable insights into the behavior of the zero-bandwidth extended Hubbard model in the strong on-site repulsion limit.

In this paper, we study the existence and properties of large conformal metrics with prescribed scalar curvature on compact Riemannian manifolds. We establish a general existence result for such metrics under certain conditions on the scalar curvature function. We also investigate the behavior of these metrics under conformal deformations and prove a rigidity result for metrics with constant scalar curvature. Our results have applications in various areas of geometry and mathematical physics, including the study of Einstein metrics and the Yamabe problem.

The paper presents a study on the existence of large conformal metrics with prescribed scalar curvature on compact Riemannian manifolds. The main result of the paper is a new existence theorem, which shows that for a certain class of Riemannian manifolds, there always exists a conformal metric with prescribed scalar curvature, under certain conditions. The paper also provides a detailed proof of this result and discusses its implications and applications in various fields of mathematics and physics, such as differential geometry and general relativity. The paper concludes with some open questions and possible future research directions.

In this paper, we study a pinning model with heavy-tailed disorder, where the disorder potential has a heavy-tailed distribution. We analyze the critical behavior of the model and investigate the effect of heavy-tailed disorder on the pinning transition. We find that the critical exponents of the model are modified by the heavy-tailed disorder, leading to a non-trivial scaling behavior. We also explore the effect of different heavy-tailed distributions on the pinning transition and observe that the critical behavior depends on the tail index of the distribution. Our results provide insights into the behavior of pinning models with heavy-tailed disorder and contribute to the understanding of the pinning transition in disordered systems.

In the paper titled "Pinning Model with Heavy Tailed Disorder", the authors investigate the behavior of a pinning model in the presence of heavy-tailed disorder. The pinning model is a mathematical model used to study the behavior of a system of particles in a disordered medium. The heavy-tailed disorder refers to a distribution of disorder strengths that has a power-law tail, indicating the presence of rare but extremely strong disorder strengths. 

The authors analyze the behavior of the pinning model using theoretical and numerical methods. They derive analytical expressions for the critical exponents characterizing the phase transitions in the system and compare them to numerical simulations. They find that the heavy-tailed disorder has a significant impact on the behavior of the system, leading to novel critical phenomena. 

The results of this study have implications for understanding the behavior of various physical systems, such as the dynamics of magnetic domains or the formation of crystal defects in materials. The findings also contribute to the broader field of statistical physics and provide insights into the behavior of disordered systems.

This paper investigates the sliding friction behavior of a power-law fluid in the hydrodynamic lubrication regime. The authors conducted experiments using a custom-built tribometer to measure the friction coefficient as a function of sliding velocity and applied load. The results show that the friction coefficient decreases with increasing sliding velocity and reaches a minimum value at a critical velocity. Additionally, the friction coefficient increases with increasing applied load. The authors propose a theoretical model based on the Reynolds equation and the power-law fluid rheology to explain the observed friction behavior. The model predicts the critical velocity and the friction coefficient as a function of sliding velocity and applied load, which are in good agreement with the experimental data. This study provides insights into the sliding friction behavior of power-law fluids in the hydrodynamic lubrication regime and can be useful for the design and optimization of lubrication systems.

This paper investigates the sliding friction behavior of a power-law fluid in the hydrodynamic lubrication regime. The power-law fluid is commonly encountered in engineering applications and understanding its friction characteristics is crucial for designing efficient lubrication systems. Experimentation is conducted to measure the sliding friction for different sliding speeds and lubricant viscosities. The experimental results are compared with theoretical predictions based on the Reynolds equation and a power-law fluid model. The study reveals that the friction coefficient decreases with increasing sliding speed and lubricant viscosity, consistent with hydrodynamic lubrication theory. However, the friction behavior also deviates from classical theory at high sliding speeds and low viscosities, indicating the influence of non-Newtonian behavior. The findings provide valuable insights into the sliding friction behavior of power-law fluids and highlight the importance of considering non-Newtonian effects in lubrication design.

This paper examines the structural limitations of learning in Massive Open Online Courses (MOOCs) by focusing on communication vulnerability and information diffusion. The authors argue that the design and structure of MOOCs can hinder effective communication and information sharing among participants, leading to limited learning outcomes. Through a case study of a popular MOOC platform, the authors analyze the network structure and communication patterns among participants. They find that certain individuals, referred to as "communication hubs," play a crucial role in information diffusion, while others, referred to as "communication isolates," have limited access to information. The authors discuss the implications of these findings for the design and facilitation of MOOCs, highlighting the need for strategies to mitigate communication vulnerability and promote equitable information diffusion. Overall, this paper contributes to the understanding of the structural limitations of learning in MOOCs and provides insights for improving the effectiveness of online learning environments.

This paper examines the structural limitations of learning in Massive Open Online Courses (MOOCs) by focusing on two main factors: communication vulnerability and information diffusion. The study analyzes the communication patterns and diffusion of information in two popular MOOCs to understand how these factors may limit the effectiveness of learning. The findings suggest that the lack of meaningful interactions and the limited reach of information within the crowd hinder the learning experience in MOOCs. The paper concludes by discussing the implications of these limitations and suggesting potential strategies to improve learning outcomes in MOOCs.

This paper explores the Khinchin-Kahane and Levy inequalities for abelian metric groups and investigates the transfer from normed (abelian semi)groups to Banach spaces. The Khinchin-Kahane inequality is a fundamental result in probability theory and functional analysis, while the Levy inequality is a generalization of the Khinchin-Kahane inequality. The authors establish these inequalities for abelian metric groups and provide a proof of the transfer from normed (abelian semi)groups to Banach spaces. The results presented in this paper have implications for various areas of mathematics, including probability theory, functional analysis, and metric geometry.

In this paper, we consider the Khinchin-Kahane and Levy inequalities for abelian metric groups and establish the transfer from normed (abelian semi)groups to Banach spaces. We prove the Khinchin-Kahane inequality for a class of abelian metric groups, extending the result from normed groups to metric groups. Furthermore, we introduce the Levy inequality for abelian metric groups and show its connection to the Khinchin-Kahane inequality. Finally, we demonstrate the transfer of these inequalities from normed (abelian semi)groups to Banach spaces, providing new insights into the relationship between metric groups and Banach spaces.

This paper explores the concept of multiactive objects and their applications in various domains. Multiactive objects are computational entities that can concurrently execute multiple activities, allowing for more efficient and flexible processing. The paper discusses the design principles and implementation techniques for multiactive objects, as well as their advantages and limitations. It also presents several case studies where multiactive objects have been successfully applied, including in distributed systems, real-time systems, and parallel computing. The findings of this research highlight the potential of multiactive objects to improve performance and scalability in various applications, and provide insights for future developments in this field.

This paper explores the concept of multiactive objects and their applications. Multiactive objects refer to objects that have multiple forms of activity and can engage in simultaneous actions and interactions. The paper examines the theoretical underpinnings of multiactive objects and their practical implications across various domains. It discusses the benefits and challenges associated with the use of multiactive objects and provides examples of their applications in areas such as robotics, human-computer interaction, and distributed systems. The paper concludes with a discussion of future research directions and potential advancements in the field of multiactive objects.

In this paper, we present a method for constructing conformal parameterizations of slices of flat Kasner spacetimes. We start by introducing the concept of conformal parameterizations and their importance in studying spacetime geometries. We then provide a brief overview of Kasner spacetimes and their properties. Next, we describe our method for constructing conformal parameterizations of slices of flat Kasner spacetimes, which involves solving a system of partial differential equations. We present numerical results for various parameter values and discuss the implications of our findings. Finally, we conclude with a discussion of future directions for research in this area. Overall, our work contributes to the understanding of the geometry of Kasner spacetimes and provides a useful tool for studying their properties.

This paper investigates the existence and properties of conformal parameterizations of slices in flat Kasner spacetimes. The authors derive necessary and sufficient conditions for a slice to have a conformal parameterization and study the behavior of the conformal factor near the boundary of the slice and for different values of the Kasner exponents. The results provide insight into the geometric structure of flat Kasner spacetimes and establish a framework for studying other classes of spacetimes.

This paper investigates the formation of a bubble from a submerged orifice. The study aims to understand the dynamics and characteristics of the bubble formation process, as well as the factors that influence it. The experimental setup involves a submerged orifice connected to a gas supply, and the bubble formation process is captured using high-speed imaging. The results show that the bubble formation process is influenced by various factors, including the gas flow rate, the size of the orifice, and the properties of the surrounding liquid. The study provides insights into the fundamental mechanisms of bubble formation and can be useful in various applications, such as bubble column reactors and underwater propulsion systems.

This paper focuses on studying the phenomenon of bubble formation from a submerged orifice. The authors conducted experiments using different orifice sizes, water heights, and flow rates to investigate the effects on bubble formation. The results showed that the size and shape of the orifice significantly influenced the bubble formation, with larger orifices resulting in larger bubbles and vice versa. Additionally, the water height and flow rate also played a role in bubble formation, with higher water heights and flow rates resulting in faster bubble formation. The authors also examined the fluid dynamics involved in bubble formation and proposed a mathematical model to describe the process. Overall, this study provides valuable insights into the formation of bubbles from submerged orifices and contributes to a better understanding of fluid dynamics in multiphase systems.

This paper presents a complete derivation of the association log-likelihood distance for multi-object tracking. The association log-likelihood distance is a measure of the similarity between two sets of tracks, and it is commonly used in multi-object tracking algorithms. The derivation starts with the definition of the association log-likelihood distance and then proceeds to derive its mathematical expression. The paper also provides a detailed explanation of the derivation steps and discusses the implications of the derived expression. The derived association log-likelihood distance is shown to be a useful tool for evaluating the performance of multi-object tracking algorithms and can be used to compare different tracking methods. Overall, this paper contributes to the understanding of the association log-likelihood distance and its application in multi-object tracking.

In multi-object tracking (MOT), the association log-likelihood distance is a commonly used metric for evaluating the performance of tracking algorithms. However, the derivation of this metric has not been well-documented in the literature. In this paper, we provide a complete derivation of the association log-likelihood distance for MOT. We start by introducing the necessary mathematical notation and definitions. We then derive the log-likelihood ratio for data association in a Bayesian framework. Next, we derive the association log-likelihood distance by maximizing the log-likelihood ratio over all possible data associations. We also discuss the limitations and assumptions of this metric. Finally, we present numerical experiments to illustrate the practical application of the association log-likelihood distance in evaluating the performance of different MOT algorithms. This paper provides a comprehensive and rigorous derivation of the association log-likelihood distance, which will be of interest to researchers and practitioners in the field of multi-object tracking.

This paper explores the connections between subriemannian geometry and algebraic geometry. Subriemannian geometry is a branch of differential geometry that studies geometric structures on submanifolds that are not necessarily Riemannian. Algebraic geometry, on the other hand, studies the geometry of solutions to polynomial equations. The paper discusses how techniques from algebraic geometry can be applied to study subriemannian structures, and vice versa. It also explores the potential applications of these connections in various fields, such as robotics and control theory. Overall, this paper aims to bridge the gap between subriemannian geometry and algebraic geometry, and highlight the potential for cross-fertilization between these two fields.

This paper explores the connections between subriemannian geometry and algebraic geometry. Subriemannian geometry, a branch of differential geometry, studies the geometric properties of curves defined on submanifolds with restrictive conditions. Algebraic geometry, on the other hand, investigates the properties of solutions to algebraic equations using tools from algebra and geometry. The paper highlights several interesting points of contact between these two fields, such as the use of algebraic techniques in studying subriemannian geometries and the application of subriemannian geometry in algebraic geometric problems. Furthermore, the paper discusses the potential for future research in exploring and bridging the gaps between these two related yet distinct areas of mathematics.

The Casimir force is a fundamental phenomenon in physics that arises from quantum fluctuations of the electromagnetic field. Accurate measurements of the Casimir force are important for testing theoretical predictions and understanding the underlying physics. In this paper, we explore the potential contributions of noncontact atomic force microscopy (NC-AFM) for future Casimir force measurements. NC-AFM is a powerful technique that allows for high-resolution imaging and manipulation of nanoscale objects without physical contact. We discuss the advantages of NC-AFM for Casimir force measurements, including its ability to measure forces in a wide range of distances and its potential for reducing systematic errors. We also discuss the challenges and limitations of using NC-AFM for Casimir force measurements, such as the need for precise calibration and the influence of surface roughness. Overall, we conclude that NC-AFM has the potential to significantly advance the field of Casimir force measurements and provide new insights into the nature of the Casimir force.

The paper explores the potential of noncontact atomic force microscopy (NC-AFM) for future measurements of the Casimir force. The Casimir force is a small but significant force that arises from quantum fluctuations, and its accurate measurement is important for understanding fundamental physical properties. The authors discuss the limitations of current measurement techniques and propose that NC-AFM, which allows for precise control of the tip-sample separation and reduces unwanted effects, could provide more accurate and reliable measurements of the Casimir force. They present theoretical simulations and experimental results supporting their argument and conclude that NC-AFM has the potential to greatly contribute to the future of Casimir force measurements.

This paper presents the observation of empty liquids and equilibrium gels in a colloidal clay system. The authors use confocal microscopy to study the structure and dynamics of the colloidal clay particles. They find that at low concentrations, the system forms an empty liquid phase, where the particles are dispersed and do not form any structure. At higher concentrations, the system transitions to an equilibrium gel phase, where the particles form a network-like structure. The authors also investigate the effect of particle size and concentration on the formation of these phases. Overall, this study provides insights into the behavior of colloidal clay systems and contributes to our understanding of the self-assembly of colloidal particles.

In this paper, the authors present their findings on the observation of empty liquids and equilibrium gels in a colloidal clay system. Using a combination of optical microscopy, rheology, and small-angle X-ray scattering techniques, the authors were able to characterize the structure and behavior of the colloidal clay particles in different concentrations and temperatures. They found that at low concentrations, the system behaved as an empty liquid, with the particles diffusing freely. As the concentration increased, the system transitioned into an equilibrium gel state, with interconnected structures formed by the clay particles. These gel structures exhibited solid-like properties, such as elasticity and the ability to maintain their shape. The authors also observed a reversible gel-sol transition by varying the temperature, confirming the equilibrium nature of the gel state. Overall, this study provides valuable insights into the behavior of colloidal clay systems, which can have important implications in various applications, including material science, geophysics, and the food industry.

This paper presents a distributed tracking algorithm for the reconstruction of graph signals. The algorithm is designed to handle large-scale graphs and is based on a consensus-based approach. The proposed algorithm is able to track the evolution of graph signals over time, even in the presence of noise and missing data. The algorithm is evaluated through simulations on various types of graphs and signal models, and the results demonstrate its effectiveness in accurately reconstructing graph signals. The proposed algorithm has potential applications in various fields, such as social network analysis, sensor networks, and image processing.

Graph signal processing has emerged as a powerful tool for analyzing complex data represented by graphs. However, reconstructing graph signals from noisy observations is a challenging task due to the inherent structure of the graphs. In this paper, we propose a distributed tracking algorithm for reconstructing graph signals based on the consensus-based optimization framework. The algorithm leverages the local information available at each node in the graph to estimate the unknown graph signal. We also analyze the convergence properties of the proposed algorithm and provide simulation results to demonstrate its effectiveness in reconstructing graph signals in different scenarios. Our algorithm offers significant advantages over existing methods by providing a distributed solution that can handle large-scale graphs in a computationally efficient manner.

In this paper, we investigate the parameter space of the spin-orbit problem, focusing on the existence and stability of normally hyperbolic invariant circles (NHICs). We provide a detailed analysis of the bifurcation diagram and identify regions in parameter space where NHICs exist. We also study the stability of these NHICs using the Melnikov method and find that they can be stable under certain conditions. Our results contribute to a better understanding of the spin-orbit problem and provide insights into the dynamics of NHICs in this system.

In this paper, we investigate the parameter space of the spin-orbit problem in celestial mechanics. Specifically, we focus on the existence of normally hyperbolic invariant circles, which are key features in the dynamics of this system. We explore the variation of these circles as the parameters of the problem change, and we analyze their stability properties. Our results provide insights into the structure and behavior of the spin-orbit problem, and contribute to the understanding of celestial mechanics in general.

This paper investigates the role of natural convection in the dissolution of sessile droplets. Sessile droplets are liquid droplets that are deposited on a solid surface and do not spread. The dissolution of these droplets is an important process in various applications, such as pharmaceuticals, food processing, and environmental monitoring. The authors conducted experiments to study the dissolution behavior of sessile droplets under different conditions, including varying droplet size, temperature, and concentration of the solute. They found that natural convection plays a significant role in the dissolution process, affecting the dissolution rate and the distribution of the solute within the droplet. The authors also developed a mathematical model to describe the dissolution process, taking into account the effects of natural convection. The results of this study provide insights into the dissolution behavior of sessile droplets and can be used to optimize processes involving droplet dissolution.

This paper presents an experimental study on the role of natural convection in the dissolution process of sessile droplets. Sessile droplets are liquid droplets that are confined on a solid surface, and dissolution refers to the process in which the droplet gradually dissipates into its surroundings. Natural convection, which is the flow of fluid due to density differences caused by temperature variations, has been found to significantly affect the dissolution rate of sessile droplets. Through a series of controlled experiments, the authors investigate the influence of various parameters, such as droplet volume, surface temperature, and ambient conditions, on the dissolution kinetics. The results demonstrate that natural convection can both enhance and hinder the dissolution process depending on the specific conditions. This study provides valuable insights into the important role of natural convection in the dissolution of sessile droplets and contributes to the understanding of mass transfer phenomena in complex fluid systems.

This paper proposes a three-detector short-baseline neutrino oscillation program in the Fermilab Booster Neutrino Beam. The program aims to study neutrino oscillations at short baselines using a combination of near, intermediate, and far detectors. The near detector will provide precise measurements of the neutrino flux and cross-sections, while the intermediate and far detectors will measure the neutrino oscillation parameters. The proposed program will provide valuable insights into neutrino oscillations and help address some of the outstanding questions in neutrino physics.

This paper presents a proposal for a three-detector short-baseline neutrino oscillation program using the Fermilab Booster Neutrino Beam. The goal of this program is to study neutrino oscillations and further understand the properties of neutrinos. The proposal outlines the design and construction of three detectors at different distances from the neutrino source, allowing for precise measurements of the neutrino oscillation parameters. The paper discusses the scientific motivations for the program, the technical details of the detectors, and the expected experimental sensitivities. The proposed program has the potential to provide valuable insights into neutrino physics and may contribute to our understanding of fundamental particles and the nature of the universe.

This paper investigates the effect of interface anisotropy on the precession of magnetization induced by laser heating. The authors demonstrate that the presence of interface anisotropy can lead to a $\pi$ phase shift in the precession of magnetization. This effect is attributed to the competition between the exchange interaction and the interface anisotropy. The authors propose a theoretical model to explain this phenomenon and validate their findings through numerical simulations. The results of this study provide insights into the dynamics of magnetization precession and have potential implications for the design of spintronic devices.

This paper explores the phenomenon of a $\pi$ phase shift induced by interface anisotropy in the precession of magnetization initiated by laser heating. The authors investigate how the interaction between light and a magnetic material can lead to a change in the magnetization dynamics, specifically a $\pi$ phase shift. They conduct experiments using a custom-built setup and demonstrate the impact of varying laser parameters on the phase shift. The results suggest that interface anisotropy plays a significant role in this phenomenon and provide insights into the underlying physics. This research contributes to the understanding of magnetization dynamics and has potential implications for applications such as data storage and spintronics.

This paper presents lower bounds on the oracle complexity of nonsmooth convex optimization problems using information theory. The oracle complexity measures the number of queries required to solve a problem using an oracle, which provides information about the objective function and its derivatives. The authors derive lower bounds on the oracle complexity for a class of nonsmooth convex optimization problems, showing that the number of queries required to solve these problems is inherently large. These lower bounds provide insights into the inherent difficulty of solving nonsmooth convex optimization problems and can guide the development of more efficient algorithms. The results are supported by theoretical analysis and numerical experiments.

This academic paper introduces lower bounds on the oracle complexity of nonsmooth convex optimization problems using information theory. The authors derive these bounds by considering the information-theoretic properties of oracles, which are used to access information about the objective function. They analyze two types of oracles: membership oracles that can determine whether a point lies in the feasible region, and comparison oracles that can compare the objective values of two points. The lower bounds are derived for the case of optimization over polytopes and extend existing lower bounds for smooth convex optimization. The authors also provide numerical examples to demonstrate the tightness of the derived bounds and discuss the implications for practical optimization algorithms. Overall, this paper contributes to the theoretical understanding of nonsmooth convex optimization and provides useful insights for the development of efficient optimization algorithms.

This paper introduces a new proof system called nested hypersequents, which combines the advantages of both nested sequents and hypersequents. Nested hypersequents allow for a more compact and intuitive representation of proofs, while still maintaining the expressive power of hypersequents. The paper presents the syntax and proof rules for nested hypersequents, and proves soundness and completeness results for the system. Additionally, the paper explores the relationship between nested hypersequents and other proof systems, such as nested sequents and hypersequents, and discusses potential applications and future directions for research in this area.

This academic paper explores the concept of grafting hypersequents onto nested sequents and proposes a new method for combining these two proof systems. Traditional nested sequents and hypersequents have distinct features and advantages, which can be leveraged to create a more versatile proof system. The paper presents a systematic approach for grafting hypersequents onto nested sequents, providing a unified framework to capture the benefits of both proof systems. The proposed method is formalized and examined through several examples, demonstrating its effectiveness and potential applications for enhancing proof search and proof structuring in automated theorem proving. Overall, this paper contributes to the advancement of proof theory and offers a valuable tool for logic researchers and practitioners.

In this paper, we investigate the interaction between $F(R,T)$ gravity and modified Chaplygin gas (MCG) in the framework of a homogeneous and isotropic universe. We derive the field equations for the $F(R,T)$ gravity with MCG and obtain the corresponding Friedmann equations. We then analyze the behavior of the scale factor and energy density for different values of the parameters in the model. We find that the interaction between $F(R,T)$ gravity and MCG can lead to interesting cosmological scenarios, such as accelerated expansion and late-time cosmic acceleration. Our results provide insights into the dynamics of the universe in the presence of $F(R,T)$ gravity and MCG, and may have implications for understanding the nature of dark energy.

The paper presents a study on the interacting $F(R,T)$ gravity theory with a modified Chaplygin gas (MCG) in the framework of homogeneous and isotropic Friedmann-Robertson-Walker (FRW) cosmology. The modified Chaplygin gas is considered as a dark energy component, while $F(R,T)$ gravity takes into account the modification of the Einstein-Hilbert action by including the trace of the energy-momentum tensor. The paper derives the modified Friedmann equations and explores the effects of the interaction term on the evolution of the universe. The results show that the interaction term affects the expansion rate, equation of state parameter, and energy density of the universe. Additionally, the paper analyzes the stability conditions, autonomous system, and critical points of the dynamical system to provide a comprehensive understanding of the interacting $F(R,T)$ gravity with modified Chaplygin gas.

This paper presents a method for the absolute calibration of fiber-coupled single-photon detectors. The calibration procedure involves measuring the detection efficiency and dark count rate of the detector using a calibrated reference source. The reference source consists of a single-photon emitter and a calibrated power meter. The calibration is performed at multiple wavelengths to account for any wavelength-dependent effects. The results show that the calibration method is accurate and reliable, with uncertainties of less than 1%. This absolute calibration allows for the accurate determination of the detection efficiency and dark count rate of fiber-coupled single-photon detectors, enabling more precise measurements in various applications such as quantum communication and quantum sensing.

This paper presents a method for the absolute calibration of fiber-coupled single-photon detectors. The calibration method is based on the measurement of the efficiency and dark count rate of the detector using a calibrated reference detector. The absolute efficiency and dark count rate of the detector are determined by comparing its performance to that of the reference detector. The calibration method is validated by measuring the performance of several fiber-coupled single-photon detectors and comparing the results to those obtained using other calibration techniques. The absolute calibration of fiber-coupled single-photon detectors is essential for accurate measurements in a wide range of applications, including quantum communication, quantum cryptography, and quantum information processing.

This paper presents a mathematical model to investigate the effects of multiple myeloma on kidney function. Multiple myeloma is a cancer of plasma cells that can lead to kidney damage and dysfunction. The model incorporates various factors such as tumor growth, immune response, and kidney function to simulate the progression of the disease and its impact on renal function. The model is validated using clinical data and can be used to predict the effects of different treatment strategies on kidney function. The results of the simulations suggest that early detection and intervention are crucial in preserving kidney function in multiple myeloma patients. This model provides a valuable tool for understanding the complex interactions between multiple myeloma and kidney function and can aid in the development of personalized treatment plans for patients.

This paper presents a modeling approach to analyze the effects of multiple myeloma on kidney function. Multiple myeloma is a cancer that affects plasma cells in the bone marrow and can lead to renal complications. The study aims to understand the underlying mechanisms by which multiple myeloma impacts kidney function and to provide insights into potential treatment strategies. A mathematical model is developed, incorporating the dynamics of plasma cell growth, cytokine production, and renal damage. The model is validated using experimental data from patients with multiple myeloma and kidney dysfunction. Simulation results show that increasing plasma cell population and cytokine production lead to progressive renal damage. The model also predicts the effectiveness of targeted therapies in mitigating kidney dysfunction. Overall, this study provides a quantitative framework for investigating the complex interactions between multiple myeloma and kidney function, offering valuable insights for clinical decision-making and drug development.

In this paper, we study the problem of random online domination of the path graph. We consider the best and worst case permutations for this problem, where the goal is to find the minimum number of vertices that need to be dominated in order to cover the entire graph. We analyze the performance of various algorithms for this problem and provide theoretical bounds on the number of dominated vertices. Our results show that the best case permutation can be achieved by a greedy algorithm, while the worst case permutation requires a more complex approach. We also discuss the implications of our findings for practical applications of random online domination in real-world networks.

In this paper, we analyze the best and worst case permutations for random online domination of the path. Online domination is a graph theoretical concept that models the process of occupying vertices of a graph in an online manner such that every vertex either belongs to the dominating set or is adjacent to a dominated vertex. The path is a particular type of graph that consists of a sequence of vertices connected by edges. We consider the random online domination problem, where vertices are occupied randomly until all vertices are dominated. We investigate the best and worst case permutations, which represent the most efficient and least efficient ways of dominating the path. Our analysis includes theoretical results and experimental simulations that provide insights into the performance of different permutations in terms of the required number of occupied vertices and the running time. We also discuss the implications of our findings for practical applications and future research directions in the field of online domination.

This paper investigates the formation of carrier field shocks in dispersive media when long wavelength femtosecond pulses are propagated. The authors use numerical simulations to study the dynamics of the carrier field and find that shocks can form due to the interplay between dispersion and self-phase modulation. The results show that the shock formation is influenced by the initial pulse shape and the dispersion properties of the medium. The findings of this study provide insights into the behavior of long wavelength femtosecond pulses in dispersive media and have implications for the design of optical devices and systems.

This paper investigates the formation of carrier field shocks in dispersive media under the influence of long wavelength femtosecond pulses. This paper presents a subspace leakage analysis and an improved direction of arrival (DOA) estimation method for scenarios with small sample sizes. The abstract for the academic paper titled "Anomalous Hall Effect in Ge(1-x-y)Pb(x)Mn(y)Te Composite System" discusses the investigation of the anomalous Hall effect (AHE) in a composite system composed of Ge(1-x-y)Pb(x)Mn(y)Te. This paper investigates the phenomenon of free particle to complex Korteweg-de Vries (KdV) breathers through isospectral deformation. The Galactic bulge is a dense region at the center of the Milky Way galaxy, and understanding its stellar populations is crucial for understanding the formation and evolution of galaxies. This paper presents a quantitative test of general theories of the intrinsic laser linewidth. The paper "On the Convex Pfaff-Darboux Theorem of Ekeland and Nirenberg" explores the convex Pfaff-Darboux theorem, which is a fundamental result in convex analysis. This paper explores the concept of pattern avoidance for set partitions using the framework introduced by Klazar. Collective chemotaxis, the directed movement of a group of cells in response to a chemical gradient, is a fundamental process in many biological systems. The authors demonstrate the effectiveness of their approach through numerical experiments on various benchmark problems. The results show that the proposed method outperforms existing dimension reduction techniques in terms of both solution quality and computational time. Overall, this paper provides a valuable contribution to the field of semidefinite programming and offers a promising avenue for future research in dimension reduction techniques.

This paper investigates the application of Jordan algebras in dimension reduction techniques for semidefinite programs (SDPs). SDPs are a class of optimization problems that arise in various practical applications, such as control theory and machine learning. The authors propose a novel approach that utilizes the algebraic structure of Jordan algebras to reduce the dimension of SDPs without loss of information. The proposed method is based on a factorization theorem for Jordan algebras and provides a way to obtain lower-dimensional representations of SDPs. The authors present theoretical results supporting the effectiveness of their approach and provide several numerical experiments to demonstrate its practical applicability. Overall, this paper contributes to the growing field of dimension reduction techniques for SDPs and highlights the potential of Jordan algebras in this context.

This paper presents a correction to the well-posedness results of semilinear stochastic wave equations with H\"{o}lder continuous coefficients. The original paper contained an error in the proof of the main theorem, which has been identified and corrected in this paper. The corrected proof establishes the existence and uniqueness of solutions to the semilinear stochastic wave equations under certain conditions on the coefficients. The corrected results provide a solid foundation for further research and applications of semilinear stochastic wave equations.

This paper presents a correction to "Well-posedness of semilinear stochastic wave equations with H\"{o}lder continuous coefficients", which was previously published. The initial publication presented a well-posedness result for these equations under certain conditions. However, it has been discovered that there was an error in the proof of one of the main theorems. This correction addresses this error and provides a corrected proof for the well-posedness result. The corrected theorem is stated and proven, and the implications of this correction are discussed.

This paper presents a method for measuring the squeezed vacuum state using a bichromatic local oscillator. The squeezed vacuum state is a quantum state of light that exhibits reduced quantum noise in one quadrature compared to the vacuum state. The authors propose a setup that combines a squeezed vacuum state with a bichromatic local oscillator to measure the squeezing parameter. They demonstrate the effectiveness of their method through experimental results, showing a high degree of accuracy in measuring the squeezing parameter. This measurement technique has potential applications in quantum information processing and quantum communication.

This paper presents a new method for measuring the squeezed vacuum state using a bichromatic local oscillator. The authors first review the theory of squeezed vacuum states and the standard methods for measuring them. They then propose a new method that uses a bichromatic local oscillator to further enhance the precision of the measurement. The authors describe the setup of the experiment, including the generation of the bichromatic local oscillator and its interaction with the squeezed vacuum state. They present the results of their measurements, comparing them to the results obtained using the standard methods. The authors conclude that the use of a bichromatic local oscillator significantly improves the precision of the measurement of squeezed vacuum states. They discuss the potential applications of this method in various fields, such as quantum information processing and quantum metrology. Overall, this paper provides a new and useful technique for measuring squeezed vacuum states, with important implications for future research in the field.

Quantum repeater networks are a crucial component for long-distance quantum communication. However, current repeater protocols suffer from limitations in terms of scalability and resource requirements. In this paper, we propose a novel approach called recursive quantum repeater networks, which addresses these limitations by utilizing a hierarchical structure of repeaters. We present a detailed analysis of the performance and resource requirements of our proposed network architecture, and compare it with existing repeater protocols. Our results demonstrate that recursive quantum repeater networks offer significant improvements in terms of scalability and resource efficiency, making them a promising solution for long-distance quantum communication.

This paper studies the use of recursive quantum repeater networks for improving the efficiency and scalability of long-distance quantum communication. Quantum repeaters are essential in extending the reach of quantum communication protocols by mitigating the inevitable loss of quantum information over long distances. The authors propose a recursive approach to the design of these repeater networks, whereby smaller-scale networks are nested within larger ones, allowing for the repeated distribution and entanglement swapping of quantum information. They introduce a recursive repeater protocol that incorporates probabilistic swapping operations and analyze its performance in terms of fidelity and communication rates. The paper also explores the impact of noise and imperfections in the repeater nodes on the overall performance. The results demonstrate the potential of recursive repeater networks in achieving highly efficient long-distance quantum communication with improved scalability.

The concept of a multiverse, where multiple universes exist alongside our own, has gained significant attention in recent years. This paper explores the idea of the multiverse as an ensemble of stable and unstable universes. We propose a framework that categorizes universes based on their stability, with stable universes being those that can sustain life and unstable universes being those that cannot. We discuss the implications of this framework for the anthropic principle and the fine-tuning of the laws of physics. Additionally, we examine the potential observational signatures of unstable universes and propose methods for detecting them. Overall, this paper provides a comprehensive analysis of the multiverse as an ensemble of stable and unstable universes, shedding light on the nature of our own universe and its place within the larger multiverse.

This paper explores the concept of the multiverse as an ensemble of stable and unstable universes. The authors propose a theoretical framework that considers the existence of multiple universes with varying degrees of stability. They argue that unstable universes may arise from the quantum fluctuations of the vacuum, leading to the creation of new universes with different physical laws. This hypothesis is supported by mathematical models and simulations, which suggest that stable universes can coexist with a myriad of unstable ones. Furthermore, the authors discuss the implications of this framework for our understanding of the origins and nature of the universe, suggesting that the multiverse may provide an explanation for the observed fine-tuning of the fundamental constants. Overall, this paper presents a novel perspective on the multiverse concept and opens up new avenues for further research in cosmology and quantum physics.

This academic paper explores the development of an interactive directory for Norfolk, Nebraska during the years 1899-1900. The directory serves as a valuable resource for researchers, historians, and individuals interested in the history of Norfolk during this time period. The paper discusses the process of creating the interactive directory, including data collection, digitization, and website development. It also examines the benefits and limitations of an interactive directory compared to traditional print directories. The paper concludes with a discussion on the potential future applications of interactive directories for historical research and preservation.

This academic paper explores the development of an interactive directory for Norfolk, Nebraska from the years 1899-1900. Uniform determinantal representations are a powerful tool in algebraic geometry and commutative algebra. In this paper, we study the concept of uniform determinantal representations and provide a comprehensive overview of the existing literature on the subject. We discuss the various properties and applications of uniform determinantal representations, including their connection to the geometry of projective varieties and their role in solving systems of polynomial equations. We also present new results and techniques for constructing uniform determinantal representations, and explore their implications for computational algebraic geometry. Overall, this paper aims to provide a thorough understanding of uniform determinantal representations and their significance in algebraic geometry and commutative algebra.

Uniform determinantal representations are a class of polynomial formulas that encode the relationship between determinants and their component variables. In this paper, we explore the properties and applications of uniform determinantal representations, including their connections to algebraic geometry and their role in solving systems of polynomial equations. We also investigate the conditions under which uniform determinantal representations exist and analyze their computational complexity. Our findings provide insights into the mathematical structure of determinantal formulas and open up new avenues for research in related fields.

This paper explores the concept of perfect NOT transformation and conjugate transformation in the context of mathematical transformations. The authors provide a comprehensive analysis of these transformations, including their properties, applications, and mathematical representations. The paper also discusses the relationship between perfect NOT transformation and conjugate transformation, highlighting their similarities and differences. The findings of this study contribute to a deeper understanding of these transformations and their potential applications in various fields of mathematics.

This paper analyzes the concept of perfect NOT transformation and conjugate transformation. The authors propose a new definition of perfect NOT transformation based on the existing definition of perfect complements. They also introduce the concept of conjugate transformation as a way to further classify perfect NOT transformations. The paper provides theoretical explanations and practical examples to illustrate the effectiveness and applicability of these transformations. The findings of this study contribute to a better understanding of the relationship between perfect complements and perfect NOT transformations, and provide a framework for further research in this field.

This paper investigates the low-frequency 1/f noise in MoS2 thin-film transistors (TFTs) by comparing single and multilayer structures. The authors fabricated MoS2 TFTs with different numbers of layers and measured their electrical characteristics and noise spectra. They found that the single-layer MoS2 TFTs exhibited lower 1/f noise compared to the multilayer structures. The authors also analyzed the noise sources and proposed a model to explain the observed behavior. This study provides valuable insights into the noise characteristics of MoS2 TFTs and offers guidance for optimizing their performance in various applications.

This academic paper investigates the low-frequency 1/f noise in MoS2 thin-film transistors, comparing single-layer and multilayer structures. MoS2 is a promising material for electronic devices due to its excellent electrical performance, but the presence of 1/f noise can limit its practical applications. The authors conducted measurements on single-layer and multilayer MoS2 transistors and analyzed the 1/f noise characteristics. They found that the 1/f noise in single-layer transistors was significantly lower compared to multilayer transistors. The authors attributed this difference to the absence of interlayer coupling in single-layer transistors. The study provides valuable insights into the nature of 1/f noise in MoS2 transistors, offering guidance for the optimization of device performance and noise reduction strategies.

This paper presents a comprehensive study on distributed clustering and learning over networks. The authors propose a novel framework that combines clustering algorithms with distributed learning techniques to enable efficient and scalable analysis of large-scale network data. The framework leverages the inherent structure of the network to distribute the computation and communication tasks among multiple nodes, thereby reducing the computational complexity and communication overhead. The authors also develop a distributed consensus algorithm that allows the nodes to collaboratively learn the underlying patterns and relationships in the network data. Experimental results on real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed framework in achieving accurate clustering and learning results. The findings of this study have significant implications for various applications in network analysis, such as social network analysis, sensor network monitoring, and distributed anomaly detection.

This paper explores the problem of distributed clustering and learning over networks. It presents a novel algorithm that combines distributed online learning with consensus clustering to handle large-scale networked data. The algorithm utilizes a divide-and-conquer strategy to assign data points to local clusters and then iteratively refines these assignments by incorporating information from neighboring clusters. The experimental results demonstrate that the proposed algorithm outperforms existing methods in terms of clustering accuracy and scalability when applied to various real-world datasets. Overall, this work contributes to the development of efficient and effective distributed clustering and learning algorithms for networked data.

This paper presents a continuously updated bibliography on the topics of superiorization and perturbation resilience of algorithms. Superiorization is a methodology that aims to improve the performance of an algorithm by adding a perturbation term to the objective function. Perturbation resilience, on the other hand, refers to the ability of an algorithm to maintain its performance in the presence of perturbations. The bibliography includes references to relevant papers, books, and other resources that discuss these topics. The goal of this bibliography is to provide researchers and practitioners with a comprehensive and up-to-date collection of resources on superiorization and perturbation resilience, facilitating further research and development in these areas.

This academic paper presents a continuously updated bibliography on the topics of superiorization and perturbation resilience algorithms. Superiorization is a mathematical framework that aims to improve the quality of solutions generated by existing algorithms, while perturbation resilience refers to the ability of algorithms to handle perturbations in the problem. The bibliography provides a comprehensive collection of papers, books, and other resources related to these topics, allowing researchers and practitioners to easily access and explore the current state of research in the field. This paper investigates the use of jet schemes for solving advection problems. Jet schemes are a class of numerical methods that approximate the solution of partial differential equations by using a Taylor series expansion. The authors propose a new jet scheme algorithm that is specifically designed for advection problems. The algorithm is tested on a variety of advection problems and compared to other numerical methods. The results show that the jet scheme algorithm is able to accurately and efficiently solve advection problems, making it a promising approach for this class of problems.

This paper investigates the use of jet schemes for the numerical solution of advection problems. Advection problems arise in various fields, such as fluid dynamics, meteorology, and traffic flow simulations. Jet schemes are a class of numerical methods that aim to capture sharp gradients and discontinuities in the solution accurately. In this study, we develop a new jet scheme algorithm and compare its performance with other existing methods. We analyze the accuracy and efficiency of the proposed scheme through numerical experiments on a set of benchmark test problems. The results demonstrate the superiority of the jet scheme in capturing sharp gradients and discontinuities, making it a promising choice for advection problems.

In this paper, we investigate the compatibility of holographic QCD with the Regge trajectories of vector and axial-vector mesons. We use a holographic model that incorporates the effects of confinement and chiral symmetry breaking. By comparing the predicted masses and slopes of the Regge trajectories with experimental data, we find that holographic QCD is able to reproduce the observed patterns. This suggests that the holographic approach provides a viable framework for understanding the spectrum of mesons in QCD. Additionally, we discuss the implications of our results for the nature of the underlying theory and the role of holography in QCD.

This paper explores the holographic Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) model and its correlation with the Regge trajectories of vectors and axial-vectors. The holographic QCD model is a theoretical framework that uses the principles of gauge/gravity duality to study the dynamics of QCD. The authors analyze the spectrum of vectors and axial-vectors in holographic QCD and compare it to the Regge trajectories observed in experimental data. They find that the holographic QCD model accurately reproduces the qualitative features of the Regge trajectories, providing further evidence for the validity of this theoretical framework. Furthermore, the authors discuss the implications of their findings for understanding the nature of strong interactions in QCD. This study contributes to the ongoing efforts to develop a comprehensive understanding of QCD and its fundamental properties.

This paper investigates the dynamic structural and topological phase transitions on the Warsaw Stock Exchange using a phenomenological approach. The authors analyze the time series data of stock prices and trading volumes to identify the presence of phase transitions in the market. They propose a novel method based on the concept of dynamic networks to capture the changing structure and topology of the market. The results show that the Warsaw Stock Exchange exhibits both structural and topological phase transitions, indicating significant changes in the market dynamics. The findings have important implications for understanding the behavior of financial markets and can potentially inform investment strategies.

This paper investigates the dynamic structural and topological phase transitions that occur on the Warsaw Stock Exchange. The study employs a phenomenological approach to analyze the fluctuations and patterns observed in the stock market using network theory. The authors identify several structural and topological changes that represent critical points in the market dynamics. They utilize a variety of statistical measures to characterize these transitions and demonstrate their significance in understanding the underlying mechanisms of the stock market. The findings contribute to the field of econophysics and provide valuable insights for investors and policymakers.

This paper explores the concept of collapse theories in quantum mechanics and their implications for the ontology of the universe. Collapse theories propose that the wave function of a quantum system collapses into a definite state upon measurement, resolving the measurement problem in quantum mechanics. However, these theories give rise to several paradoxes, such as the quantum Zeno effect and the quantum sleeping beauty problem. The paper argues that these paradoxes can be resolved by adopting a primitive ontology approach, which posits that the fundamental entities of the universe have definite properties and exist independently of observation. The paper concludes by discussing the implications of this approach for our understanding of the nature of reality and the role of consciousness in quantum mechanics.

This paper provides an analysis of the philosophical implications of collapse theories in quantum mechanics. It explores the paradoxes that arise in these theories and evaluates their impact on our understanding of the nature of reality. The paper also examines the concept of primitive ontology and its relevance for collapse theories. By examining the ontological commitments of collapse theories, the paper aims to contribute to the ongoing debate on the foundations of quantum mechanics. The analysis in this paper suggests that collapse theories present both exciting possibilities for resolving the measurement problem in quantum mechanics and significant challenges for our understanding of the fundamental nature of the universe.

Protein aggregation is a phenomenon that occurs when proteins misfold and form insoluble aggregates, leading to various neurodegenerative diseases. Understanding the underlying mechanisms of protein aggregation is crucial for developing effective therapeutic strategies. In this paper, we present a statistical mechanical approach to studying protein aggregation. We use a combination of theoretical modeling and computer simulations to investigate the thermodynamics and kinetics of protein aggregation. Our results provide insights into the factors that influence protein aggregation, such as protein concentration, temperature, and the presence of co-solvents. Additionally, we propose a novel theoretical framework that describes the formation and growth of protein aggregates. This work contributes to the field of protein aggregation research and may aid in the development of new therapeutic interventions for neurodegenerative diseases.

This paper presents a statistical mechanical approach to understanding protein aggregation, a phenomenon that is the hallmark of numerous neurodegenerative diseases. The authors develop a model based on statistical mechanics principles to investigate the thermodynamics and kinetics of protein aggregation. They utilize concepts such as free energy landscapes, transition state theory, and reaction rate constants to characterize the aggregation process. The model is able to accurately predict various experimental observations and provides insights into key factors that influence protein aggregation, such as protein concentration, temperature, and molecular interactions. This approach offers a quantitative framework for studying protein aggregation and may facilitate the development of new strategies for preventing or treating neurodegenerative diseases associated with aberrant protein aggregation.

This paper presents a typology and profiling framework for human-machine networks. Human-machine networks refer to the interconnected systems where humans and machines collaborate to achieve a common goal. The proposed typology categorizes human-machine networks based on the level of human-machine interaction and the degree of autonomy of the machines. The profiling framework aims to capture the characteristics and capabilities of the human and machine components in a network. The typology and profiling framework provide a systematic approach for understanding and analyzing human-machine networks, which can be useful for designing and optimizing such networks in various domains.

This paper proposes a typology and profiling framework for human-machine networks. Human-machine networks are systems that involve collaborations between humans and machines, and such collaborations are becoming increasingly prevalent in various domains. However, there is a lack of theoretical frameworks to categorize and analyze these networks. In this paper, we first present a typology that classifies human-machine networks into four categories based on the level of human participation and machine autonomy. We then propose a profiling framework that characterizes the important features of each category. The profiling framework includes dimensions such as decision-making authority, information processing capabilities, and interface design. This framework provides a systematic way to analyze and compare different human-machine networks. We demonstrate the practical utility of our typology and profiling framework through a case study on autonomous vehicles. Overall, this paper contributes to the understanding of human-machine networks and provides a basis for future research and design in this area.

This paper investigates the yielding and flow behavior of aggregated particulate suspensions. The study focuses on understanding the mechanisms that govern the transition from a solid-like to a fluid-like behavior in these suspensions. The authors use a combination of experimental and numerical techniques to characterize the rheological properties of the suspensions and to elucidate the underlying physical processes. The results show that the yielding behavior is influenced by the size and shape of the aggregates, as well as the concentration and nature of the suspending medium. The flow behavior is found to be governed by the interplay between the interparticle forces and the hydrodynamic interactions. The findings of this study contribute to a better understanding of the flow behavior of aggregated particulate suspensions and have implications for various industrial applications, such as the processing of granular materials and the design of flow control devices.

This paper explores the yielding and flow behavior in aggregated particulate suspensions. The formation of aggregates in suspensions is a common phenomenon, and understanding their rheological properties can have important implications in various industrial processes. The study applies advanced experimental techniques, such as rheology and microscopy, to investigate the effects of various factors, including aggregate size, concentration, and inter-particle forces, on the yielding and flow behaviors of the suspensions. The results provide insights into the mechanisms governing the rheological properties of aggregated suspensions and offer guidelines for optimizing their flow behavior in practical applications. Overall, this research contributes to the fundamental understanding of yield stress and flow in particulate suspensions containing aggregates, which has practical significance in a variety of fields, such as food processing, pharmaceuticals, and cosmetic industries.

This paper introduces a new method for computing bordered Floer homology for manifolds with torus boundary using immersed curves. Bordered Floer homology is a powerful tool in symplectic topology that allows for the study of the symplectic geometry of manifolds with boundary. The authors develop a framework for constructing immersed curves in these manifolds and use them to define a new version of bordered Floer homology. They prove that this new version is isomorphic to the traditional bordered Floer homology, providing a more efficient and computationally tractable method for its computation. The paper concludes with several examples and applications of this new method in symplectic topology.

This paper investigates the bordered Floer homology for manifolds with torus boundary using the framework of immersed curves. Specifically, it develops a construction for computing the bordered Floer homology which takes into account the torus boundary. The main results of this paper include the computation of bordered Floer homology for certain torus bundles over surfaces, as well as the establishment of a spectral sequence for manifolds with torus boundary. The paper also addresses the relationship between bordered Floer homology and the Heegaard Floer homology, providing a comparison between the two theories. These results contribute to a deeper understanding of the bordered Floer homology for manifolds with torus boundary and give new insights into the topological properties of these manifolds.

This paper examines the continuous-time portfolio choice problem under monotone mean-variance preferences in the presence of stochastic factors. The authors develop a dynamic optimization framework to solve the problem and derive the optimal investment strategy. They also analyze the impact of various factors, such as risk aversion and market conditions, on the optimal portfolio allocation. The results show that the optimal strategy depends on the investor's risk aversion and the characteristics of the stochastic factors. The findings provide insights into the optimal portfolio choice for investors with monotone mean-variance preferences in a stochastic environment.

This paper investigates the continuous-time portfolio choice problem under monotone mean-variance preferences in the presence of stochastic factors. The authors consider a general stochastic factor model where asset returns are driven by common and idiosyncratic factors. They derive the explicit form of the optimal portfolio policy using dynamic programming techniques and provide conditions for the existence and uniqueness of the optimal solution. The results show that the optimal portfolio policy is influenced by the investor's risk aversion, as well as the correlation structure between the assets and the factors. Additionally, the authors examine the impact of transaction costs on the optimal portfolio policy and discuss the implications for real-world investment decisions. Overall, this study contributes to the understanding of portfolio choice under uncertainty and provides practical insights for investors.

This paper presents a modeling and simulation study on the effects of cyclic loading on the formation of articular cartilage lesions. The study aims to understand the underlying mechanisms of lesion formation and provide insights into potential preventive measures. A finite element model of the knee joint is developed, incorporating the mechanical properties of articular cartilage and the loading conditions experienced during cyclic activities. The model is validated using experimental data and then used to simulate the effects of different loading parameters on lesion formation. The results show that cyclic loading can lead to the development of cartilage lesions, with higher loading magnitudes and frequencies resulting in more severe lesions. The study also investigates the role of cartilage thickness and composition in lesion formation. Overall, the findings contribute to a better understanding of the biomechanics of articular cartilage and provide a basis for future research on preventive strategies for cartilage lesions.

This paper presents a modeling and simulation study on the effects of cyclic loading on articular cartilage lesion formation. Articular cartilage plays a critical role in joint functionality, and improper loading can lead to the development of lesions. The researchers developed a computational model that simulates the mechanical behavior of articular cartilage under cyclic loading conditions. The model incorporates various factors such as stress distribution, fluid flow, and tissue deformation. The simulations were performed to investigate how different loading patterns and magnitudes affect the formation and progression of cartilage lesions. The results reveal insights into the complex mechanisms behind cartilage lesion formation and provide a basis for understanding and potentially preventing these conditions. This study demonstrates the potential of computational models in elucidating the intricate biomechanical processes involved in articular cartilage pathology.

This paper investigates the power of arc consistency for constraint satisfaction problems (CSPs) defined by partially-ordered forbidden patterns. The authors propose a new algorithm called Partially-Ordered Arc Consistency (POAC) that extends the traditional arc consistency algorithm to handle partially-ordered constraints. They prove that POAC is sound and complete for CSPs defined by partially-ordered forbidden patterns. The authors also conduct experiments to compare the performance of POAC with other arc consistency algorithms on various benchmark problems. The results show that POAC outperforms the other algorithms in terms of runtime and solution quality. Overall, this paper demonstrates the effectiveness of arc consistency for CSPs defined by partially-ordered forbidden patterns and highlights the potential of POAC as a powerful algorithm for solving such problems.

Arc consistency is a powerful technique used to efficiently solve constraint satisfaction problems (CSPs). In this paper, we investigate the application of arc consistency to CSPs defined by partially-ordered forbidden patterns. We present a novel algorithm that establishes arc consistency for these types of CSPs and prove its correctness. Our algorithm is based on a depth-first search approach and incorporates a heuristic for efficient variable ordering. We also provide experimental results demonstrating the effectiveness of our approach on a set of benchmark problems. Our findings suggest that arc consistency is a valuable tool for solving CSPs defined by partially-ordered forbidden patterns, providing significant improvements in both computational efficiency and solution quality.

This paper investigates the concept of rational sets in Euclidean spaces and spheres. A rational set is defined as a set that can be expressed as the solution set of a system of rational equations. The authors explore the properties and characteristics of rational sets in both Euclidean spaces and spheres. They provide examples and counterexamples to illustrate the behavior of rational sets in different dimensions. The paper also discusses the relationship between rational sets and algebraic varieties, and presents some results on the intersection of rational sets with other geometric objects. Overall, this paper contributes to the understanding of rational sets in Euclidean spaces and spheres, and provides insights into their geometric properties.

This paper investigates the concept of rational sets in Euclidean spaces and spheres. A rational set is defined as a set that can be constructed using a finite number of rational numbers and operations such as addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division. The authors examine various properties of rational sets, including closure under these operations and under the taking of complements.
