This paper presents a novel approach for segmenting manifold valued images using active contour models. Manifold valued images are a type of data representation that can capture complex structures and relationships in high-dimensional data. The proposed method extends traditional active contour models to handle manifold valued images by incorporating a Riemannian metric and a geodesic distance function. The active contour model is formulated as an energy minimization problem, which is solved using an iterative optimization algorithm. Experimental results on various manifold valued image datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of the proposed method compared to existing segmentation techniques. The proposed approach has potential applications in medical imaging, computer vision, and other fields where manifold valued images are commonly encountered.

The paper "Active Contour Models for Manifold Valued Image Segmentation" presents a novel approach for segmenting manifold valued images using active contour models. Manifold valued images are a type of data representation that capture complex structures and relationships in multi-dimensional information. The proposed method extends traditional active contour models to handle manifold valued images by introducing a new energy functional and incorporating manifold geometry. Experimental results on a variety of real-world examples demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of the proposed approach compared to existing methods. The research contributes to the field of image segmentation and provides new insights into handling complex data structures in computer vision applications.

This paper evaluates the accuracy of Maximum a Posteriori (MAP) segmentation using hidden Potts and Markov mesh prior models. The authors compare three different algorithms: Path Constrained Viterbi Training, Iterated Conditional Modes, and Graph Cut based algorithms. The results show that all three algorithms achieve high accuracy in segmenting images, with the Path Constrained Viterbi Training algorithm performing the best. These findings suggest that incorporating hidden Potts and Markov mesh prior models can improve the accuracy of MAP segmentation.

This academic paper investigates the accuracy of MAP segmentation using hidden Potts and Markov mesh prior models through the application of Path Constrained Viterbi Training, Iterated Conditional Modes, and Graph Cut based algorithms. The study compares the performance of these algorithms using various metrics to evaluate the segmentation accuracy. The results show that all three algorithms are effective in achieving accurate segmentation, but the Graph Cut based algorithm outperforms the others in terms of accuracy. These findings contribute to the field of segmentation algorithms and provide insights for further improvement in this area.

This paper presents a large-margin metric learning approach for partitioning problems. Partitioning problems involve dividing a set of objects into multiple subsets based on certain criteria. The proposed approach aims to learn a distance metric that maximizes the margin between different subsets, thereby improving the accuracy of partitioning. The authors formulate the problem as a convex optimization task and propose an efficient algorithm to solve it. Experimental results on various real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach in improving the performance of partitioning algorithms. The large-margin metric learning approach has the potential to be applied in various domains, such as clustering, classification, and recommendation systems.

Large-Margin Metric Learning for Partitioning Problems is an academic paper that proposes a novel approach for solving partitioning problems by utilizing large-margin metric learning. Partitioning problems involve dividing a set of objects into multiple disjoint subsets based on certain criteria, and this paper focuses on finding an optimal partitioning solution through metric learning. The paper introduces the concept of large-margin metric learning, which aims to maximize the pairwise margin between objects in different partitions while minimizing the margin within the same partition. The authors propose a specific algorithm for large-margin metric learning in the context of partitioning problems and demonstrate its effectiveness through empirical evaluations on various real-world datasets. The results indicate that the proposed approach results in improved partitioning solutions compared to existing methods, highlighting the potential of large-margin metric learning in solving partitioning problems.

This paper presents a method for segmenting ultrasound images of thyroid nodules to assist in fine needle aspiration cytology. The proposed method utilizes a combination of image processing techniques, including thresholding, morphological operations, and region growing, to accurately identify the boundaries of the nodule. The segmented images can then be used to extract features that can aid in the diagnosis of thyroid nodules. The effectiveness of the proposed method is evaluated using a dataset of ultrasound images of thyroid nodules, and the results demonstrate its ability to accurately segment the nodules. The proposed method has the potential to improve the efficiency and accuracy of fine needle aspiration cytology for the diagnosis of thyroid nodules.

This paper focuses on the development of a segmentation method for ultrasound images of thyroid nodules that can aid in assisting in fine needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) procedures. The proposed method incorporates a combination of image processing techniques to accurately delineate the boundaries of the thyroid nodule in ultrasound images. The segmentation method includes pre-processing steps to enhance the image quality, followed by region-based segmentation algorithms to correctly classify the nodule region. The performance of the proposed method was evaluated using a dataset of ultrasound images of thyroid nodules, and the results were compared with manual segmentations by expert radiologists. The experimental results show that the proposed method achieves high accuracy in segmenting the thyroid nodules, thereby providing valuable assistance in the FNAC procedure. The segmentation method has the potential to improve the accuracy and efficiency of thyroid nodule diagnosis, leading to better patient outcomes.

This paper presents a non-parametric convolution based image-segmentation method for ill-posed objects using a context window approach. The proposed method aims to overcome the challenges of segmenting objects with complex shapes and unclear boundaries. The method utilizes a convolution operation to extract local features from the image and applies a context window approach to incorporate global information. Experimental results on various datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in accurately segmenting ill-posed objects. The proposed method shows promising potential for applications in computer vision and image processing tasks.

This paper proposes a non-parametric convolution based image-segmentation method for ill-posed objects. The method incorporates a context window approach to improve the accuracy and reliability of the segmentation results. The approach utilizes convolution operations on local image patches and considers the contextual information of neighboring pixels to make informed segmentation decisions. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in accurately segmenting ill-posed objects in images. The non-parametric nature of the method makes it applicable to a wide range of object shapes and sizes, making it a valuable tool in computer vision and image analysis applications.

This paper presents a novel image segmentation enhancement technique that combines active contour and topological alignments. The proposed technique aims to improve the accuracy and efficiency of image segmentation by incorporating topological information into the active contour framework. The technique first initializes the active contour using a region-based approach and then refines the contour using topological alignments. Experimental results on various datasets demonstrate that the proposed technique outperforms existing methods in terms of segmentation accuracy and computational efficiency. The proposed technique has potential applications in various fields such as medical imaging, object recognition, and computer vision.

Image segmentation is a crucial step in computer vision and image analysis applications. This paper presents a novel image segmentation enhancement technique based on active contour and topological alignments. The proposed method first uses an active contour model to obtain an initial segmentation of the image. Then, a topological alignment algorithm is applied to refine the segmentation by aligning the contour with the boundaries of the objects in the image. Experimental results on various image datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed technique in improving the accuracy and robustness of image segmentation. The proposed method outperforms existing state-of-the-art algorithms in terms of segmentation accuracy and computational efficiency. This enhancement technique has the potential to be widely used in various computer vision applications, such as object detection, image recognition, and medical image analysis.

This paper presents a comparative study of statistical skin detection algorithms for sub-continental human images. Skin detection is an important task in various computer vision applications, such as face detection, gesture recognition, and adult content filtering. However, existing skin detection algorithms are often designed and evaluated on datasets that are biased towards certain ethnic groups, leading to poor performance on sub-continental human images. In this study, we evaluate and compare the performance of five state-of-the-art statistical skin detection algorithms on a diverse dataset of sub-continental human images. We analyze the algorithms' performance in terms of accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 score, and investigate the impact of dataset bias on their performance. Our results show that the performance of the algorithms varies significantly across different sub-continental groups, highlighting the need for more inclusive and diverse datasets for training and evaluating skin detection algorithms. This study provides valuable insights for researchers and practitioners working on skin detection algorithms for sub-continental human images.

Skin detection is a crucial step in many computer vision applications such as face detection and recognition, nudity detection, and human tracking. However, existing skin detection algorithms are often designed and tested on datasets that are biased towards a specific population, limiting their effectiveness on images of people from different regions or ethnicities. This paper presents a comparative study of statistical skin detection algorithms for sub-continental human images, specifically focusing on images of people from South Asia, East Asia, and Africa. The study evaluates the performance of seven popular skin detection algorithms using a diverse dataset of images collected from these regions. The algorithms are compared based on their precision, recall, and F1 scores, and the robustness of each algorithm to variations in lighting conditions, image resolution, and skin tones is assessed. The results of this study provide insights into the strengths and limitations of existing skin detection algorithms for sub-continental human images, and can guide the development of more accurate and inclusive skin detection algorithms for a wide range of computer vision applications.

This paper investigates the influence of intensity standardization on the accuracy and robustness of medical image registration. The results show that the proposed method significantly improves the accuracy and robustness of image registration, leading to more reliable and consistent alignment of medical images. This paper investigates the influence of intensity standardization on the accuracy of medical image registration. Medical image registration is an essential task in various medical applications, including diagnosis, treatment planning, and image fusion. However, the accuracy of registration highly depends on the intensity characteristics of the input images. Intensity standardization methods aim to reduce the intensity differences between images to improve registration accuracy. This study compares various intensity standardization techniques, including histogram matching, global intensity scaling, and local intensity normalization, on a dataset of medical images. The results demonstrate that intensity standardization can significantly improve the accuracy of medical image registration. The findings from this study have implications for improving the performance of medical image registration algorithms and ultimately enhancing the quality of medical diagnosis and treatment.

This paper presents a comprehensive review of physical modeling techniques used in active contours for image segmentation. Active contours, also known as snakes, are widely used in computer vision and image processing for object detection and boundary extraction. The paper discusses various physical modeling techniques, including energy minimization, deformable models, and level set methods. It also explores the advantages and limitations of each technique and provides insights into their applications in different image segmentation tasks. The review aims to provide researchers and practitioners with a better understanding of the physical modeling techniques used in active contours and their potential for improving image segmentation accuracy and efficiency.

This paper presents a review of physical modeling techniques used in active contours for image segmentation. Active contours are deformable models that adjust their shape to delineate objects of interest in an image. Physical modeling techniques aim to incorporate physical properties such as elasticity and mass into the contour models, enabling more accurate and robust segmentation. The paper provides an overview of different physical modeling techniques, including the level-set method, the viscous fluid model, and the deformable mesh model. The advantages and limitations of each technique are discussed, along with their applications in various fields. The paper also highlights current challenges and future directions in physical modeling techniques for active contours in image segmentation. This review provides a valuable resource for researchers working in the field of image processing and computer vision.

This paper presents polynomial time algorithms for solving bi-criteria, multi-objective, and ratio problems in clustering and imaging. Specifically, the authors focus on the normalized cut and ratio regions. The normalized cut problem aims to partition a graph into two sets such that the cut between the sets is minimized and the sizes of the sets are balanced. The ratio region problem involves finding a region in an image that maximizes the ratio of the sum of the intensities inside the region to the sum of the intensities outside the region. The authors propose efficient algorithms for solving these problems, providing theoretical analysis and experimental results to demonstrate their effectiveness. Overall, this work contributes to the development of efficient algorithms for important problems in clustering and imaging.

This paper presents polynomial time algorithms for addressing bi-criteria, multi-objective, and ratio problems in clustering and imaging. Specifically, the authors focus on the normalized cut and ratio regions problems. The normalized cut problem aims to minimize the value of a cut while also minimizing the number of clusters. The ratio regions problem, on the other hand, seeks to find a partition that maximizes the ratio of the between-cluster variation to the within-cluster variation. The authors propose efficient algorithms that provide approximate solutions to these problems. The efficacy of the algorithms is demonstrated through experimental results on both synthetic and real datasets. Overall, the paper provides valuable insights into the computational aspects of bi-criteria, multi-objective, and ratio problems in clustering and imaging.

Boosting algorithms are a popular class of machine learning algorithms that combine weak learners to create a strong learner. The dual formulation of boosting algorithms has been proposed as an alternative to the traditional primal formulation. In this paper, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the dual formulation of boosting algorithms. We show that the dual formulation offers several advantages over the primal formulation, including improved convergence rates and better generalization performance. We also propose a novel dual boosting algorithm and demonstrate its effectiveness through extensive experiments on various datasets. Our results suggest that the dual formulation of boosting algorithms has the potential to significantly enhance the performance of boosting algorithms in practice.

Boosting algorithms have become a popular approach for solving various machine learning problems. In this paper, we investigate the dual formulation of boosting algorithms, which has been less studied compared to the primal formulation. We first derive the dual form of some well-known boosting algorithms, such as AdaBoost and Gradient Boosting. We then analyze the relationship between the primal and dual formulations, showing that they are dual to each other in a certain sense. Next, we propose a new boosting algorithm based on the dual formulation, called DualBoost. Experimental results on several benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of DualBoost compared to other state-of-the-art boosting algorithms. Finally, we discuss the advantages and limitations of the dual formulation of boosting algorithms and provide directions for future research.

In this paper, we present a method for the exact two-dimensionalization of low-magnetic-Reynolds-number flows subject to a strong magnetic field. We derive a set of equations that describe the flow in two dimensions, taking into account the effects of the magnetic field. We then solve these equations numerically to obtain the exact two-dimensional solution for the flow. We demonstrate the accuracy of our method by comparing our results with experimental data and show that our method provides a good approximation for the flow in the presence of a strong magnetic field. Our method has potential applications in various fields, including magnetohydrodynamics and plasma physics.

In this paper, we present an exact two-dimensionalization approach for studying low-magnetic-Reynolds-number flows in the presence of a strong magnetic field. We derive the two-dimensional Navier-Stokes-Maxwell equations by neglecting the transverse velocity and magnetic field components. We then show that these reduced equations accurately capture the behavior of the flow at these low Reynolds and magnetic Reynolds numbers. We validate our approach by comparing the two-dimensionalized solution with the full three-dimensional solution for various flow configurations. Our results demonstrate the applicability and accuracy of the two-dimensionalization approach for studying such flows. This approach provides a useful framework for analyzing and understanding low-magnetic-Reynolds-number flows in the presence of a strong magnetic field, and can be extended to more complex and realistic systems.

The abstract for the academic paper titled "Effect of electron irradiation on superconductivity in single crystals of Ba(Fe$_{1-x}$Ru$_{x}$)$_2$As$_2$ ($x=$0.24)" is as follows:

This academic paper investigates the effect of electron irradiation on the superconductivity properties of Ba(Fe$_{1-x}$Ru$_{x}$)$_2$As$_2$ single crystals with a Ru concentration of $x=$0.24. The results suggest that electron irradiation can be used as a tool to manipulate the superconducting properties of Ba(Fe$_{1-x}$Ru$_{x}$)$_2$As$_2$ single crystals, which may have implications for the development of new superconducting materials and devices.

This paper explores the use of state machines in large-scale computer software and systems. The paper discusses the benefits of using state machines in software development, including improved modularity, maintainability, and testability. It also presents various techniques for implementing state machines in large-scale systems, such as hierarchical state machines and statecharts. State machines are widely used in computer software and systems to model and control the behavior of complex systems. However, as software systems grow in size and complexity, traditional state machine models become difficult to manage and analyze. In this paper, we present a novel approach to state machines for large scale computer software and systems. This paper investigates graded comodule categories with enough projectives. We define graded comodules and graded comodule categories, and study their properties. We show that if a graded comodule category has enough projectives, then it is equivalent to the category of graded modules over a graded coalgebra. We also provide examples of graded comodule categories with enough projectives. Finally, we discuss the relationship between graded comodule categories and graded module categories.

This paper studies graded comodule categories with enough projectives, which are categories equipped with a grading structure and a structure of comodules over a coalgebra. We show that under certain conditions, the category of graded comodules over a coalgebra has enough projectives, which means that every object can be embedded into a projective object. We also investigate the relationship between graded comodule categories with enough projectives and other categories, such as graded module categories and comodule categories without grading. This paper presents an in-situ Raman study of laser-induced graphene oxidation. Laser-induced graphene (LIG) is a promising material for various applications due to its unique properties. However, the oxidation of LIG can significantly affect its performance. In this study, we investigate the oxidation process of LIG using Raman spectroscopy. We observe the formation of various oxygen-containing functional groups on the LIG surface during the oxidation process. The intensity of the D and G bands in the Raman spectra decreases with increasing oxidation time, indicating the reduction of sp2 carbon content. Additionally, we observe the formation of a new peak at around 1700 cm-1, which is attributed to the presence of carboxyl groups. Our results provide valuable insights into the oxidation process of LIG and can guide the development of strategies to control and optimize the oxidation process for specific applications.

Laser-induced graphene (LIG) has gained significant attention for its potential applications in various fields including energy storage, sensing, and electronics. One important aspect of LIG is its oxidation behavior, which can significantly affect its properties and performance. In this study, we investigate the oxidation process of LIG using in-situ Raman spectroscopy. Through a series of experiments, we demonstrate that the intensity ratio of the D and G peaks in the Raman spectrum can be used as a reliable indicator of the oxidation level of LIG. Furthermore, we investigate the effect of different laser powers and exposure times on the oxidation kinetics of LIG. Our results provide valuable insights into the oxidation behavior of LIG, and pave the way for the development of improved synthesis and processing techniques for this promising material.

In this paper, we present a comprehensive review of the shape dynamics description of gravity. Shape dynamics is a novel approach to understanding the nature of gravity that aims to provide a background-independent formulation of the theory. We discuss the key ideas and concepts behind shape dynamics, including the role of conformal transformations and the emergence of spacetime geometry. We also explore the implications of shape dynamics for the cosmological constant problem and the black hole information paradox. Finally, we discuss the current status of shape dynamics research and potential future directions. Overall, this paper provides a thorough overview of the shape dynamics description of gravity and its implications for our understanding of the fundamental nature of the universe.

The paper presents a comprehensive and rigorous description of gravity using the framework of shape dynamics. Shape dynamics is a reformulation of general relativity that eliminates the need for absolute space and time, and instead treats the metric of spacetime as a physically meaningful field. The authors develop the mathematical formalism of shape dynamics and demonstrate its equivalence to general relativity in the appropriate limit. They also discuss the implications of shape dynamics for black holes and cosmology, showing how it provides a unified description of gravitational phenomena. By providing a new perspective on gravity, this work opens up new avenues for research and sheds light on the fundamental nature of spacetime.

This paper presents a data processing method for atomic resolution electron energy-loss spectroscopy (EELS) data. The method involves several steps, including background subtraction, energy calibration, and spectrum averaging. The background subtraction is performed using a polynomial fitting algorithm, while the energy calibration is achieved by comparing the EELS data with a reference spectrum. The spectrum averaging is carried out to improve the signal-to-noise ratio. The effectiveness of the proposed method is demonstrated through experiments on various materials. The results show that the method can effectively process atomic resolution EELS data and provide accurate and reliable spectral information. This method has the potential to greatly enhance the analysis of atomic-scale chemical and electronic structures using EELS.

Electron energy-loss spectroscopy (EELS) is a valuable technique for analyzing the electronic structure and chemical composition of materials at the atomic scale. However, the high spatial and energy resolutions of modern EELS instruments generate vast amounts of data that can be challenging to process and analyze. In this paper, we propose a novel data processing approach for atomic resolution EELS datasets. Our method utilizes advanced algorithms for denoising, background subtraction, and spectral decomposition, enabling accurate extraction of the fine atomic features in the EELS spectra. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by applying it to experimental datasets acquired on various materials. The results illustrate the ability of our method to enhance the signal-to-noise ratio, separate overlapping spectral contributions, and provide valuable insights into the local electronic and chemical properties of the studied samples. The proposed data processing framework promises to advance the capabilities of atomic resolution EELS and facilitate its application in diverse scientific fields.

This paper presents a novel approach for sub 20 nm silicon patterning and metal lift-off using thermal scanning probe lithography (t-SPL). The t-SPL technique utilizes a heated probe to locally heat the resist material, enabling precise control over the patterning process. The authors demonstrate the feasibility of sub 20 nm patterning by fabricating silicon nanostructures with dimensions as small as 10 nm. Additionally, the paper explores the use of t-SPL for metal lift-off, a critical step in the fabrication of nanoscale devices. The results show that t-SPL can achieve high-resolution metal patterning with excellent lift-off efficiency. Overall, this work presents a promising approach for sub 20 nm silicon patterning and metal lift-off, offering potential applications in nanoelectronics and nanophotonics.

This paper introduces a novel approach to silicon patterning and metal lift-off using thermal scanning probe lithography. The technique involves utilizing a heated nanoscale probe to locally heat and de-passivate a silicon surface, enabling the controlled formation of nanoscale patterns. These patterns can then be used as templates for metal lift-off processes, allowing for the precise fabrication of sub-20 nm metal structures. The authors demonstrate the feasibility of this approach through experiments and discuss the potential applications and advantages of thermal scanning probe lithography in nanofabrication. Overall, this research presents a promising technology for high-resolution patterning and nanoscale metal fabrication in various fields, including electronics and photonics.

This paper presents a scalable approach to solving worst-case linear discriminant analysis (WLDA) problems using semidefinite programming (SDP) techniques. WLDA is a popular method for classification tasks, but its computational complexity limits its applicability to large datasets. The authors propose a reformulation of WLDA as a semidefinite feasibility problem, which can be efficiently solved using SDP solvers. Experimental results demonstrate the scalability and effectiveness of the proposed approach on various datasets, making it a promising tool for large-scale classification problems.

We propose a new approach to solve the worst-case linear discriminant analysis (LDA) problem using scalable semidefinite feasibility problems. LDA is a popular method for dimensionality reduction and classification, but traditional methods often suffer from computational difficulties with large datasets. Our proposed method utilizes semidefinite programming to efficiently solve large-scale LDA problems, resulting in a scalable and computationally efficient solution. We provide theoretical analysis and experimental results to demonstrate the effectiveness and scalability of our approach. Overall, our method offers a promising solution to the challenging problem of worst-case LDA using scalable semidefinite feasibility problems.

This paper investigates the Cauchy problem for elliptic complexes in spaces of distributions. The authors establish the existence and uniqueness of solutions to the Cauchy problem for elliptic complexes in the space of distributions. They also provide a characterization of the regularity of solutions in terms of the regularity of the initial data. The results are applied to the study of the Cauchy problem for elliptic systems of partial differential equations. The paper concludes with some examples illustrating the main results.

This paper investigates the Cauchy problem for elliptic complexes in spaces of distributions. The Cauchy problem is an initial value problem in which the evolution of a system is determined by its initial conditions. Our main goal is to establish well-posedness results for the Cauchy problem in various function spaces. We consider the case of elliptic complexes, which are systems of partial differential equations that satisfy certain ellipticity conditions. We show that under suitable assumptions on the coefficients of the complex, the Cauchy problem has a unique solution in spaces of distributions. Our results generalize and improve upon previous work in this area. Additionally, we discuss the existence and uniqueness of weak solutions, and provide examples to illustrate the applicability of our results. Overall, this paper contributes to the understanding of the Cauchy problem for elliptic complexes, and provides a foundation for further study in this field.

Phase unwrapping is a critical step in many imaging applications, including interferometry and synthetic aperture radar. In this paper, we propose a novel isotropic inverse-problem approach for two-dimensional phase unwrapping. Our method is based on the assumption that the phase is smooth and can be represented as a sum of a low-frequency component and a high-frequency component. We formulate the phase unwrapping problem as a regularized least-squares optimization problem and solve it using an iterative algorithm. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world data. Our method outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques in terms of accuracy and robustness, making it a promising solution for phase unwrapping in various imaging applications.

Phase unwrapping is a crucial step in many imaging techniques, including interferometry and synthetic aperture radar. In this paper, we propose a new approach for two-dimensional phase unwrapping using an isotropic inverse-problem formulation. We model the unwrapped phase as a two-dimensional signal and solve an optimization problem to estimate the unwrapped phase map. Our approach is based on the assumption of isotropy, which allows us to simplify the problem and reduce computational complexity. We evaluate the performance of our method on synthetic and real data, and compare it to existing methods. The results show that our approach achieves accurate phase unwrapping with improved computational efficiency. Additionally, we demonstrate the robustness of our method to noise and discontinuities in the phase map. Overall, our approach provides a novel and efficient solution for two-dimensional phase unwrapping, with potential applications in various imaging domains.

This paper presents a novel approach, called the $\Delta$-Machine Learning approach, that combines big data and quantum chemistry approximations to improve the accuracy and efficiency of quantum chemistry calculations. The $\Delta$-Machine Learning approach leverages the power of machine learning algorithms to learn the differences between accurate quantum chemistry calculations and approximate methods. By training on a large dataset of accurate quantum chemistry calculations, the $\Delta$-Machine Learning approach can then predict the differences between approximate and accurate calculations for new molecules. This allows for the rapid and accurate estimation of quantum chemistry properties for a wide range of molecules, without the need for computationally expensive accurate calculations. The paper demonstrates the effectiveness of the $\Delta$-Machine Learning approach through a series of experiments on various molecular systems, showing significant improvements in accuracy and efficiency compared to traditional quantum chemistry approximations. Overall, the $\Delta$-Machine Learning approach has the potential to revolutionize the field of quantum chemistry by enabling the rapid and accurate estimation of quantum chemistry properties for large-scale molecular systems.

In this paper, we propose a new approach called the $\Delta$-Machine Learning Approach, which combines big data and quantum chemistry approximations. We demonstrate how large data sets can be used to train machine learning models to accurately predict quantum chemistry properties. This approach not only improves the accuracy of traditional quantum chemistry approximations, but also reduces the computational cost. We employ a new feature extraction method to convert data points from a high-dimensional space to a low-dimensional space, allowing for efficient analysis and modeling. We validate the effectiveness of the $\Delta$-Machine Learning Approach on several benchmark data sets and compare the results with existing quantum chemistry approximations. The experimental results show that our approach outperforms existing methods in terms of accuracy and efficiency. Overall, the $\Delta$-Machine Learning Approach has the potential to revolutionize quantum chemistry research by enabling more accurate and scalable simulations.

This paper explores the mathematical concept of square-tiled tori, which are two-dimensional surfaces that can be represented as a square grid with identified edges. The authors provide a comprehensive overview of the theory and properties of square-tiled tori, including their classification, symmetries, and topological properties. They also discuss various applications of square-tiled tori in different areas of mathematics, such as number theory and dynamical systems. The paper concludes with open questions and future directions for research in this field. Overall, this paper serves as a valuable resource for mathematicians interested in the study of square-tiled tori and their applications.

This paper explores the mathematical properties of square-tiled tori, which are two-dimensional surfaces consisting of square tiles arranged in a periodic pattern. The authors investigate various aspects of square-tiled tori, including their topological properties, tiling spaces, and geometric properties. They also discuss the relationship between square-tiled tori and other mathematical structures, such as flat structures and billiards. The paper provides a comprehensive overview of square-tiled tori and their relevance in various areas of mathematics.

This paper presents a novel approach for generating robust cluster states using the principles of reduce, reuse, and recycle. The authors propose a method that reduces the number of resources required for cluster state generation, reuses existing resources whenever possible, and recycles unused resources for future use. The proposed approach is evaluated through extensive simulations and compared with existing methods. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of the reduce, reuse, and recycle approach in generating robust cluster states while minimizing resource consumption. This paper contributes to the field of quantum computing by providing a more efficient and sustainable method for cluster state generation.

In quantum computing, cluster states play a critical role in various quantum information processing tasks. However, the generation of cluster states requires a challenging process that often leads to high failure rates and resource inefficiencies. In this paper, we propose a new method, called "Reduce, reuse, recycle," that significantly enhances the generation of cluster states. By exploiting the inherent symmetries in the cluster state generation process, we demonstrate how to reduce the number of necessary entangling gates, reuse existing quantum gates, and recycle failed attempts to improve success rates. Through extensive simulations and experiments, we show that our method not only achieves higher success rates but also consumes fewer resources compared to existing approaches. These findings provide valuable insights for developing more robust and efficient cluster state generation techniques in quantum computing.

This paper investigates the characteristics of the Eliashberg formalism by studying the high-pressure superconducting state in phosphor. The Eliashberg formalism is a theoretical framework used to describe the behavior of superconducting materials. The authors analyze the electronic structure and phonon spectrum of phosphor under high pressure conditions and use these results to calculate the superconducting properties of the material. The study reveals the importance of electron-phonon interactions in the superconducting state and provides insights into the mechanisms behind high-pressure superconductivity in phosphor. The findings contribute to a better understanding of the Eliashberg formalism and its application in the study of superconducting materials.

The Eliashberg formalism is a theoretical tool commonly used to investigate the properties of superconducting materials. In this paper, we examine the characteristics of the Eliashberg formalism through the analysis of the high-pressure superconducting state in phosphor. We discuss how the formalism allows us to understand the behavior of the superconducting state under different conditions, such as varying levels of applied pressure. We also explore how the formalism can be used to predict and analyze various properties of the superconducting state, including critical temperature and energy gap. Overall, our findings demonstrate the effectiveness of the Eliashberg formalism in studying superconducting materials and provide valuable insights into the high-pressure superconducting state in phosphor.

This paper investigates the phenomenon of sticky seeding in discrete-time reversible-threshold networks. Sticky seeding refers to the tendency of certain nodes in a network to consistently remain in a particular state, even when the network dynamics would suggest otherwise. The authors propose a mathematical model to analyze and predict the occurrence of sticky seeding in such networks. They also present simulation results to validate their model and demonstrate the impact of various network parameters on the prevalence of sticky seeding. The findings of this study contribute to a better understanding of the dynamics of reversible-threshold networks and have implications for the design and control of such systems.

This paper introduces a new seeding algorithm for discrete-time reversible-threshold networks, referred to as sticky seeding. The algorithm leverages the inherent reversibility of the network to selectively seed nodes that have high influence on the network dynamics. The effectiveness of sticky seeding is evaluated through extensive simulations on various network topologies and with different thresholds. The results demonstrate that sticky seeding significantly improves the spread of information, compared to traditional random seeding methods. The algorithm is also shown to be robust against various perturbations and is scalable to large networks. Ultimately, sticky seeding has the potential to enhance the efficiency of information diffusion in real-world systems, such as social networks and epidemiological models.

In this paper, we investigate the existence and properties of static solutions for nonminimally coupled topological-defect boson stars. We consider a scalar field theory with a nonminimal coupling to gravity and study the effects of this coupling on the formation and stability of boson stars. We find that the nonminimal coupling can significantly affect the properties of the boson stars, including their mass, size, and stability. We also explore the parameter space of the theory and identify regions where stable boson star solutions exist. Our results provide new insights into the formation and properties of topological-defect boson stars in the presence of a nonminimal coupling to gravity.

In this paper, we investigate the properties of nonminimally coupled topological-defect boson stars. We consider a system consisting of a self-gravitating complex scalar field with a nonminimally coupled potential in the presence of a global topological defect. We derive the field equations and study their static solutions. We find that the nonminimally coupled potential leads to new features in the properties of the boson stars. Specifically, we find that the curvature of the topological defect affects the size and mass of the boson star, and the nonminimally coupled potential leads to an increase in the maximum mass and compactness. We also study the stability of these solutions and find that they are stable under small perturbations. Overall, our results provide insight into the properties of nonminimally coupled topological-defect boson stars and their stability.

In this paper, we study the long-term behavior of solutions to the nonautonomous 3D Navier-Stokes equations. We prove the existence of a uniform global attractor, which is a compact set that attracts all bounded solutions as time goes to infinity. We also establish the uniform boundedness of the attractor, meaning that its size does not depend on the initial conditions. Our results provide a deeper understanding of the dynamics of the nonautonomous 3D Navier-Stokes equations and have implications for the stability and convergence of numerical methods for solving these equations.

The paper presents the concept of uniform global attractors for the nonautonomous 3D Navier-Stokes equations. It demonstrates the existence and uniqueness of solutions for these equations, and investigates the long-term behavior of these solutions. The authors establish the convergence of solutions to a uniform global attractor, which is a compact set that captures the long-term dynamics of the system. The paper also provides a detailed analysis of the properties of the uniform global attractor, such as its regularity and dimension. These results contribute to the understanding of the dynamic behavior of the nonautonomous 3D Navier-Stokes equations and have implications in various fields such as fluid mechanics and mathematical physics.

This paper presents a method for constructing set-valued fundamental diagrams (SVFDs) from jamiton solutions in second order traffic models. SVFDs provide a more accurate representation of traffic flow by accounting for the uncertainty and variability in traffic conditions. The proposed method utilizes the concept of jamiton solutions, which are a combination of jam and shock waves, to model traffic flow. The authors demonstrate the effectiveness of their method through numerical simulations and compare the results with traditional fundamental diagrams. The findings suggest that SVFDs constructed from jamiton solutions can better capture the complex dynamics of traffic flow and provide valuable insights for traffic management and control.

The paper introduces a novel approach for constructing set-valued fundamental diagrams (SVFDs) in second order traffic models using jamiton solutions. The study aims to provide a better understanding of traffic dynamics and improve the accuracy of traffic modeling and prediction. The proposed approach is based on the analysis of jamiton solutions, which are traffic patterns characterized by a combination of synchronized flow and congestion. By combining the SVFDs constructed from these solutions with empirical observations, the authors show that the approach can capture unique features of traffic flow and improve the accuracy of flow-density relationships. The results indicate that the proposed approach has potential for enhancing traffic management strategies and improving traffic flow efficiency.

This paper presents a formal framework for reasoning about the behavior of programming languages that include delimited-control operators with dynamic prompt generation. Delimited-control operators are a powerful tool for managing control flow in programming languages, but their behavior can be difficult to reason about due to their non-local effects. The framework introduced in this paper is based on the notion of environmental bisimulations, which provide a way to compare the behavior of two programs in terms of their observable effects. The paper defines a notion of bisimulation for programming languages with delimited-control operators and dynamic prompt generation, and proves that this notion is a congruence, meaning that it respects the compositionality of programs. The paper also presents a number of examples to illustrate the use of the framework and discusses its potential applications in program analysis and verification.

This paper presents a theoretical framework for studying the behavior of delimited-control operators with dynamic prompt generation in an environmental setting. We introduce the notion of environmental bisimulations to capture the interaction between prompts and the environment, and provide a sound and complete characterization of bisimilarity. We also develop a bisimulation proof technique that allows for reasoning about programs with dynamic prompt generation, and prove the soundness and completeness of the technique. We illustrate the usefulness of our framework by applying it to a case study involving a program with dynamic prompt generation and an environmental observer. Our results show that environmental bisimulations provide a powerful tool for analyzing the behavior of delimited-control operators with dynamic prompt generation in an environmental setting, and can facilitate the design and verification of such operators in practical programming languages.

This paper investigates the phenomenon of crossovers induced by discrete-time quantum walks. Quantum walks are a fundamental concept in quantum information theory and have been extensively studied in the context of continuous-time quantum walks. However, the study of discrete-time quantum walks and their potential to induce crossovers has received less attention. In this paper, we present a theoretical framework for analyzing crossovers induced by discrete-time quantum walks and provide numerical simulations to support our findings. We show that discrete-time quantum walks can indeed induce crossovers and discuss the implications of this phenomenon for quantum information processing. Our results contribute to a better understanding of discrete-time quantum walks and their potential applications in quantum computing and quantum algorithms.

In this paper, we investigate the behavior of discrete-time quantum walks and their ability to induce crossovers between different quantum states. We show that by carefully tuning the parameters of the quantum walk, it is possible to induce crossovers between different states with high probability. We provide a detailed analysis of the dynamics of the quantum walk and derive the conditions under which crossovers occur. Our results have implications for quantum algorithms and quantum information processing, as crossovers can be used to manipulate and control quantum states. We also discuss the potential applications of quantum crossover phenomena in various fields such as quantum computing and quantum simulation.

Quantum state tomography is a crucial tool for characterizing and verifying the performance of quantum systems. In this paper, we propose a method for qubit state tomography in superconducting circuits using weak measurements. We demonstrate that weak measurements can provide accurate and efficient estimation of the qubit state, even in the presence of measurement errors and decoherence. We present a detailed theoretical analysis of the method and provide experimental results to validate its effectiveness. Our findings suggest that weak measurements can be a valuable tool for qubit state tomography in superconducting circuits, offering improved accuracy and efficiency compared to traditional methods.

In this paper, we present a method for quantum state tomography of qubits in a superconducting circuit using weak measurements. We demonstrate that weak measurements can yield sufficient information to reconstruct the complete density matrix of the qubit state, even in the presence of measurement errors and system decoherence. We further show how to extract the coherence properties of the qubit state from the weak measurement data. Our results highlight the potential of weak measurement techniques for accurate and efficient quantum state tomography in superconducting circuits.

Quantum memories are an essential component of quantum computing systems, as they allow for the storage and retrieval of quantum information. Trapped-ion qubits are a promising platform for quantum memories, but they are susceptible to errors caused by various noise sources. In this paper, we propose a method for improving the performance of trapped-ion-qubit memories by using code-mediated error-channel balancing. We demonstrate that this technique can effectively mitigate errors caused by both coherent and incoherent noise sources, leading to a significant improvement in the fidelity of the stored quantum information. Our results suggest that code-mediated error-channel balancing can be a valuable tool for enhancing the performance of trapped-ion-qubit memories and advancing the field of quantum computing.

Trapped-ion qubits are promising candidates for quantum computing, but they suffer from significant errors due to coupling with environmental noise. In this paper, we propose a method to improve the memory performance of trapped-ion qubits by employing code-mediated error-channel balancing. We demonstrate that by encoding the qubit states in a larger Hilbert space, we can effectively suppress certain error channels and reduce the overall error rate. Our approach involves implementing a simple two-qubit code and applying an error-channel balancing procedure during the measurement step. Through numerical simulations, we show that the proposed method successfully enhances the qubit memory performance and achieves a significant reduction in errors. This work provides a practical approach for improving the reliability and fidelity of trapped-ion qubit memories, which is crucial for the successful implementation of large-scale quantum computing systems.

This paper presents an active set algorithm for estimating parameters in generalized linear models with ordered predictors. The algorithm is designed to handle situations where the number of predictors is large and the predictors are ordered. The algorithm iteratively updates the active set of predictors and estimates the parameters using a modified Newton-Raphson method. The performance of the algorithm is evaluated through simulation studies and compared to other existing methods. The results show that the proposed algorithm performs well in terms of estimation accuracy and computational efficiency. Overall, the active set algorithm provides a useful tool for estimating parameters in generalized linear models with ordered predictors.

This paper presents an active set algorithm for estimating parameters in generalized linear models with ordered predictors. The algorithm is designed to handle cases in which predictors are ordered and represent ordinal variables, such as Likert scale responses. The algorithm uses an iterative procedure to update both the parameter estimates and the active set of predictors, which are determined based on their contribution to the model fit. The performance of the algorithm is evaluated through simulations and compared to other existing methods. The results demonstrate that the proposed algorithm provides accurate and efficient parameter estimates, particularly in cases with a large number of predictors. The algorithm can be used in various fields where generalized linear models with ordered predictors are commonly employed, such as psychology, social sciences, and health research.

This paper explores the question of when a physical system can be considered to be computing. It argues that computation is not solely dependent on the physical properties of a system, but also on the interpretation and intention of the observer. The paper proposes a framework for understanding computation that takes into account both the physical and interpretive aspects of a system. It also discusses the implications of this framework for the field of computer science and the study of artificial intelligence. Overall, the paper aims to contribute to the ongoing debate about the nature of computation and its relationship to physical systems.

This academic paper titled "When does a physical system compute?" explores the fundamental question of when a physical system can be considered to be performing computation. The authors examine various perspectives and definitions of computation from the fields of computer science, physics, and philosophy, and propose a framework for determining when a physical system can be said to be engaging in computational processes. They argue that a comprehensive understanding of computation should take into account both the theoretical nature of computation and the physical implementation of computational processes. Through a detailed analysis of key concepts such as information processing, input-output relations, and causal structure, the authors develop a rigorous framework that can be used to identify instances of computation in physical systems. The paper concludes with a discussion of the implications of this framework for fields such as artificial intelligence, quantum computing, and the philosophy of mind, highlighting the importance of a unified approach to understanding computation across different disciplines. Overall, this paper provides valuable insights into the nature and boundaries of computation in physical systems, offering a foundation for further research and interdisciplinary dialogue.

This paper investigates the convergence rates of distributed Nesterov-like gradient methods on random networks. The authors propose a distributed algorithm that combines the Nesterov acceleration technique with a gossip-based communication protocol. They analyze the convergence rates of this algorithm under different network topologies and show that it achieves faster convergence compared to existing distributed gradient methods. Theoretical analysis and numerical experiments are provided to support the findings. The results of this study have implications for the design and optimization of distributed machine learning algorithms.

The paper investigates the convergence rates of distributed Nesterov-like gradient methods on random networks. The authors analyze two scenarios: a centralized scenario where all agents can communicate directly with each other, and a decentralized scenario where agents can only communicate with their immediate neighbors. They establish upper bounds on the convergence rates in both cases and provide numerical experiments to validate their theoretical results. The findings suggest that the proposed distributed Nesterov-like gradient methods achieve similar convergence rates to their centralized counterparts, highlighting their potential for scalable optimization in large-scale networked systems.

This paper explores the connections between modular functors, cohomological field theories, and topological recursion. Modular functors are mathematical objects that encode the symmetries of certain physical systems, while cohomological field theories provide a framework for studying the algebraic structures associated with these systems. The authors show that there is a deep relationship between these two concepts, and that topological recursion can be used to compute certain quantities associated with modular functors and cohomological field theories. The paper presents several examples and applications of these ideas, demonstrating their usefulness in various areas of mathematics and physics. Overall, this work contributes to our understanding of the interplay between modular functors, cohomological field theories, and topological recursion, and opens up new avenues for further research in these areas.

This paper explores the connection between modular functors, cohomological field theories, and topological recursion. Modular functors are algebraic structures that provide a way to organize and categorize certain mathematical objects called modular tensor categories. Cohomological field theories are a class of mathematical models that describe the behavior of topological field theories. Topological recursion is a mathematical method that can be used to compute certain quantities in complex analysis and quantum field theory. The authors investigate how these concepts intersect and how they can be used to study the behavior of cohomological field theories through the lens of modular functors. They also introduce new applications of topological recursion in this context. The results presented in this paper provide new insights into the mathematical structures and techniques that underlie the study of cohomological field theories.

This paper presents a comprehensive study on the non-LTE radiative transfer in cool stars, focusing on the theory and applications to the abundance analysis for 24 chemical elements. The authors develop a detailed theoretical framework for non-LTE radiative transfer in cool stars, taking into account various physical processes such as collisional excitation, ionization, and recombination. They then apply this framework to analyze the abundances of 24 chemical elements in a sample of cool stars, using observational data from high-resolution spectroscopy. The results show that the non-LTE effects are significant for many elements, leading to revised abundance determinations compared to LTE assumptions. The authors discuss the implications of these findings for our understanding of stellar evolution and nucleosynthesis processes. Overall, this study provides a valuable contribution to the field of stellar astrophysics and highlights the importance of considering non-LTE effects in abundance analysis for cool stars.

The abstract for the academic paper titled "Non-LTE radiative transfer in cool stars. Theory and applications to the abundance analysis for 24 chemical elements" presents an overview of the study's objectives, methodologies, and findings. The paper explores the use of non-local thermodynamic equilibrium (non-LTE) radiative transfer models in the analysis of chemical abundances in cool stars. The authors provide a comprehensive theoretical framework for non-LTE radiative transfer and discuss its applications for the analysis of abundances for 24 different chemical elements. They present detailed calculations and compare their results with those obtained using LTE models. The findings demonstrate the importance and accuracy of non-LTE radiative transfer models for precise abundance determinations in cool stars, particularly for elements with strong spectral lines. This paper contributes to the advancement of abundance analysis techniques in stellar astrophysics.

This paper investigates the time complexity of synchronizing discrete pulse-coupled oscillators on trees. The authors analyze the behavior of these oscillators and propose a mathematical model to describe their synchronization process. They then derive upper bounds on the time complexity of achieving synchronization on trees of different sizes. The results show that the time complexity increases exponentially with the size of the tree, highlighting the challenges of synchronizing large networks of oscillators. The findings of this study contribute to the understanding of synchronization dynamics in complex systems and have implications for the design and optimization of synchronization algorithms in various applications.

This paper investigates the time complexity of synchronizing discrete pulse-coupled oscillators on trees. The authors introduce a model for pulse-coupled oscillators on trees and analyze the time complexity of synchronizing these oscillators. They present a new algorithm for achieving synchronization and provide an analysis of its time complexity. The authors also compare their algorithm with existing ones and discuss the advantages and limitations of their approach. The findings of this research contribute to the understanding of synchronization in pulse-coupled oscillators on trees and can have implications for various applications in fields such as biology, physics, and computer science.

The paper investigates the concept of clique-width in graph theory and aims to identify minimal classes of graphs with unbounded clique-width. The authors define clique-width as a measure of the complexity of a graph and explore the relationship between clique-width and the presence of certain induced subgraphs. By identifying a finite set of forbidden induced subgraphs, the authors are able to define minimal classes of graphs with unbounded clique-width. The paper provides a theoretical framework for understanding the complexity of graphs and offers insights into the structure of graphs with unbounded clique-width.

Clique-width is a graph parameter that measures the structural complexity of a graph. In this paper, we study the minimal classes of graphs of unbounded clique-width, which are defined by finitely many forbidden induced subgraphs. We provide a complete characterization of these classes of graphs, showing that they are exactly the ones that exclude certain well-known graphs, such as cycles and complete bipartite graphs, as induced subgraphs. Our results provide insight into the structural complexity of graphs and contribute to the understanding of clique-width as a graph parameter.

This paper introduces a coalgebraic framework for reasoning about infinite traces in computer systems. The authors propose a notion of coalgebraic infinite traces, which captures the behavior of a system over an infinite sequence of states. They show that this notion can be used to reason about bisimilarity and simulation relations between systems. The authors also introduce the concept of Kleisli simulations, which provide a way to reason about systems with non-deterministic behavior. They demonstrate the usefulness of their framework by applying it to several examples, including a case study on the behavior of a concurrent system. Overall, this paper provides a novel approach to reasoning about infinite traces in computer systems, and offers new insights into the behavior of complex systems.

This paper introduces the concept of coalgebraic infinite traces and explores their applications in analyzing and simulating complex systems. The authors provide a formal definition for coalgebraic infinite traces and develop a framework for studying their properties, such as determinism, termination, and bisimulation. The authors also show how coalgebraic infinite traces can be used to model and simulate a wide range of systems, including probabilistic systems and non-deterministic systems. The paper concludes with a discussion on the advantages and limitations of using coalgebraic infinite traces as a tool for system analysis and simulation. Overall, this paper contributes to the field of formal methods and provides a new perspective on modeling and analyzing complex systems.

This paper presents a study on Minkowski measurability criteria for compact sets and relative fractal drums in Euclidean spaces. The authors introduce a new concept called relative fractal drums, which are subsets of Euclidean spaces that exhibit self-similarity and have a fractal dimension. They then propose a set of criteria based on Minkowski measures to determine the Minkowski measurability of these sets. The authors provide theoretical proofs and examples to demonstrate the effectiveness of their criteria. The findings of this study contribute to the understanding of Minkowski measurability and provide a framework for analyzing the fractal properties of compact sets and relative fractal drums in Euclidean spaces.

This paper introduces Minkowski measurability criteria for compact sets and relative fractal drums in Euclidean spaces. The Minkowski dimension, Minkowski content, and Minkowski lower and upper densities are defined in relation to compact sets. The paper explores the similarities and differences between Minkowski and Hausdorff dimensions, providing examples to illustrate the concepts. The criteria for Minkowski measurability are established, leading to the definition of relative fractal drums. The paper concludes with a discussion on the implications and applications of the Minkowski measurability criteria in the study of fractal geometry.

Salient object detection is a challenging task in computer vision, especially in the wild where images contain complex backgrounds and multiple objects. In this paper, we propose a novel approach called Inner and Inter Label Propagation (IILP) for salient object detection in the wild. The proposed method leverages both inner and inter label propagation to effectively capture the salient regions in an image. Inner label propagation is used to refine the initial saliency map by considering the local consistency of saliency values. Inter label propagation, on the other hand, utilizes the global consistency of saliency values across multiple images to further enhance the saliency map. Experimental results on benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed IILP method outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of both accuracy and robustness. The proposed method shows promising potential for salient object detection in real-world scenarios.

Salient object detection is an important task in computer vision, as it provides valuable information for various applications such as image understanding and content-based image retrieval. In this paper, we propose a novel approach for salient object detection in the wild, which combines inner label propagation and inter label propagation. Inner label propagation captures the inner correlations within each salient region, while inter label propagation captures the relationships between different salient regions. Our approach utilizes a graph-based framework, where the image is represented as a graph and the salient regions are represented as nodes. We formulate the salient object detection problem as a graph labeling problem and solve it by iteratively propagating the labels. Experimental results on several benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in handling complex scenes and achieving accurate salient object detection.

This paper presents a study on the design of robust controllers for regular linear systems with infinite-dimensional exosystems. The authors propose a new approach based on the use of a robust control framework to handle uncertainties and disturbances in the system. The proposed controllers are designed to ensure stability and performance in the presence of these uncertainties. The effectiveness of the proposed approach is demonstrated through numerical simulations and comparisons with existing methods. The results show that the proposed controllers outperform existing methods in terms of stability and performance. Overall, this paper provides a valuable contribution to the field of robust control for regular linear systems with infinite-dimensional exosystems.

This paper proposes a robust controller design for regular linear systems with infinite-dimensional exosystems. The exosystems are described using infinite-dimensional Liapunov's equations, and the controller design problem is cast as an H∞ control problem. The proposed controller design scheme ensures robust stability and performance by effectively eliminating the disturbances induced by the exosystems. The effectiveness of the proposed approach is validated through numerical simulations, which demonstrate the improved robustness and performance of the designed controller compared to existing methods. Overall, this paper contributes to the area of control systems by providing a robust control design technique for regular linear systems with infinite-dimensional exosystems.

This paper explores the concept of S-folds and their relationship to 4-dimensional N=3 superconformal field theories (SCFTs). S-folds are a generalization of T-folds, which are non-geometric backgrounds in string theory. The authors provide a detailed analysis of the properties and symmetries of S-folds, including their relation to N=3 SCFTs. They also discuss the construction of S-folds using gauged linear sigma models and provide explicit examples. The paper concludes with a discussion of the implications of S-folds for the study of string theory and SCFTs. Overall, this paper contributes to our understanding of S-folds and their role in the study of 4-dimensional N=3 SCFTs.

This paper investigates S-folds, a class of supersymmetric deformations of four-dimensional N=4 super Yang-Mills theories which break supersymmetry down to N=3. The authors provide a detailed analysis of the properties and characteristics of S-folds, including their moduli spaces and conformal invariance. The paper also explores the implications of S-folds for the AdS/CFT correspondence and holography, highlighting their potential significance for understanding the duality between gravity in five dimensions and superconformal field theories in four dimensions. Overall, this paper contributes to the theoretical understanding of N=3 superconformal field theories, providing new insights and avenues for further research in the field.

This technical report presents a method for computing compressive temporal higher order cyclostationary statistics. Cyclostationary statistics are widely used in signal processing applications for analyzing non-stationary signals. However, computing these statistics can be computationally expensive, especially for high-dimensional signals. In this report, we propose a compressive sensing approach to reduce the computational complexity of computing cyclostationary statistics. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method through simulations and provide guidelines for choosing the compressive sensing parameters. Our approach offers a promising solution for efficiently computing cyclostationary statistics in practical signal processing applications.

This technical report discusses a method for computing and exploiting higher order cyclostationary statistics in the context of compressive temporal signal processing. The proposed approach aims to capture the cyclostationary nature of signals, which is important in many applications such as signal detection and classification. The report presents an algorithm for estimating the higher order cyclic statistics of a time-domain signal using compressed sensing techniques. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in capturing the cyclostationary features of signals with a reduced number of measurements. The report concludes by highlighting the potential applications and future directions for this research.

In this paper, we investigate the complementary relation between quantum coherence and quantum correlations in multiple measurements. We consider a system composed of multiple qubits and study the behavior of coherence and correlations under different measurement scenarios. We find that there exists a trade-off between coherence and correlations, such that an increase in coherence leads to a decrease in correlations and vice versa. We provide a quantitative measure for this trade-off and show that it holds for various types of measurements. Our results shed light on the fundamental connection between coherence and correlations in quantum systems and have implications for the design and optimization of quantum information processing tasks.

This paper investigates the complementary relationship between quantum coherence and quantum correlations in multiple measurements. The authors present a theoretical framework that describes the joint behavior of these two quantum phenomena. They demonstrate that, in certain scenarios, the presence of coherence can enhance the amount of quantum correlations observed in multiple measurements, while in other scenarios, coherence and correlations exhibit a trade-off relationship. The authors also provide experimental evidence supporting their theoretical findings. This work sheds light on the intricate interplay between coherence and correlations in quantum systems, with implications for areas such as quantum information processing and quantum metrology.

The Gaussian core model is a widely used model in statistical physics to study the behavior of particles in high dimensions. In this paper, we investigate the properties of the Gaussian core model in high dimensions and provide a comprehensive analysis of its thermodynamic and structural properties. We derive analytical expressions for the equation of state and the radial distribution function, and compare our results with numerical simulations. Our findings show that the Gaussian core model exhibits interesting phase behavior in high dimensions, including the presence of a liquid-gas phase transition. We also discuss the implications of our results for other models in statistical physics and suggest possible directions for future research. Overall, our study provides valuable insights into the behavior of particles in high dimensions and contributes to the understanding of complex systems in statistical physics.

The Gaussian core model is a widely used model in statistical physics and machine learning for studying complex systems in both low and high dimensions. In this paper, we investigate the behavior of the Gaussian core model specifically in high dimensions. We derive an expression for the partition function and analyze its properties in the limit of large dimensions. We find that the system exhibits a phase transition at a critical temperature, and we determine the critical exponent characterizing this transition. We also study the behavior of the correlation functions and find that they exhibit long-range correlations in high dimensions. Our results provide new insights into the behavior of the Gaussian core model in high dimensions and have implications for understanding the behavior of complex systems in real-world applications.

This paper presents recent results in semileptonic B decays obtained from the BaBar experiment. The BaBar detector, located at the SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory, has been used to study the decays of B mesons produced in electron-positron collisions. The focus of this paper is on semileptonic decays, where one of the decay products is a charged lepton (electron or muon) and the other is a neutrino. The results presented include measurements of branching fractions, form factor parameters, and other observables related to semileptonic B decays. These measurements provide valuable information for testing the predictions of the Standard Model and searching for new physics effects.

This paper presents recent results in semileptonic B meson decays obtained from experiments conducted with the BaBar detector at the Stanford Linear Accelerator Center. The analysis focuses on the measurement of the decay rates and asymmetries of various B meson decay channels involving a lepton and a neutrino. These studies provide valuable information on fundamental properties of the weak interaction and test the predictions of the Standard Model. The results presented in this paper are based on a large dataset collected during the BaBar experiment and demonstrate the precision capabilities of the detector. The measurements are consistent with previous measurements and theoretical predictions, providing further support for the understanding of weak decays and the properties of B mesons.

This paper presents a complexity analysis of multicell coordinated beamforming with a rate outage constraint. The authors propose a novel algorithm that optimizes the beamforming vectors in a multicell system while ensuring a certain rate outage constraint. The complexity of the proposed algorithm is analyzed and compared with existing algorithms. Simulation results show that the proposed algorithm achieves a lower complexity while maintaining a similar performance compared to existing algorithms. The findings of this study provide valuable insights for the design and implementation of multicell coordinated beamforming systems.

This paper presents a complexity analysis of multicell coordinated beamforming with a rate outage constraint. The goal is to optimize the beamforming weights in a multiuser multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) system to maximize the overall system throughput while ensuring a target rate outage probability. The authors propose a novel algorithm based on semidefinite relaxation and coordinate descent techniques.
